title: Barabbas: The Man Who Walked Free Instead of Jesus
paragraphs: Barabbas: The Man Who Walked Free Instead of Jesus
They called his name.
Not Jesus.
Barabbas.

A man of violence.
A man of rebellion.
A man with blood on his hands and judgment over his head.
And yet when the moment came... he walked free.
Jesus did not.
Read that again.
Barabbas walked free. Jesus went to the cross.

That is not a side detail in the Gospel story.
That is the Gospel story.
Because Barabbas is not just a man in the crowd.
Barabbas is you.

You were the guilty one.
You were the rebel.
You were the one who had broken God’s law, resisted His rule, loved your sin, and stood condemned before a holy Judge.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23

Not some.
Not the worst.
All.

You may not have held a dagger like Barabbas.
But you held bitterness.
You held lust.
You held pride.
You held secret unbelief.
You held your own life like it belonged to you.
God saw it.
You knew.
And here is what most people do: they compare themselves to other sinners so they can avoid the terror of standing before a holy God. But heaven does not grade on a curve.
“The wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23

That means your sin is not small.
It is treason.
It is cosmic rebellion.
It is not merely a mistake.
It is guilt.
And Barabbas knew what guilt felt like.

He knew chains.
He knew iron bars.
He knew the sound of soldiers approaching.
He knew what it meant to wait for judgment.
Can you picture it?

A dark cell.
The stench of stone and sweat.
The weight of coming execution.
Every breath heavy with the knowledge that justice is near.

No argument left.
No defense left.
No innocence left.
Then footsteps.
Then voices.
Then a name.
“Barabbas.”
Maybe he thought it was the walk to death.
Maybe he expected the final humiliation.
But instead, impossible words reached his ears:
He was being released.
Why?
Because another man would take his place.
Not just any man.
Jesus.

The sinless Son of God.
The spotless Lamb.
The only truly innocent Man standing in Jerusalem that day.

Pilate knew Jesus had done nothing deserving death.
The crowd knew Barabbas was guilty.
And yet they cried for the guilty man to go free and the righteous One to be crushed.
“Now at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would. And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas.” — Matthew 27:15–16
“But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus.” — Matthew 27:20
Do you see it?

The wicked is released.
The righteous is condemned.
The guilty walks away.
The innocent is led to slaughter.
That is substitution.
That is the shadow of the cross before the nails even pierce His hands.
“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows… he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities… and with his stripes we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:4–5

For our transgressions.
For our iniquities.
Not His.
He had none.

Barabbas deserved the cross on Golgotha.
Jesus carried it.

You deserved wrath.
Jesus drank it.

You deserved judgment.
Jesus stood in it.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

The crowd choosing Barabbas over Jesus is not just a moment in history.
It is the human heart exposed.
Because people still choose Barabbas.

They choose rebellion over surrender.
Self over Christ.
Sin over holiness.
Darkness over light.
“And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light…” — John 3:19

That is your natural condition apart from grace.
Not neutral.
Not “basically good.”
Not spiritually trying your best.
Dead in sin.
“And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.” — Ephesians 2:1

Dead people do not rescue themselves.
Dead religion cannot raise a dead soul.
Good works cannot erase guilt.
Church attendance cannot remove wrath.
Trying harder cannot make you clean.
Only Jesus saves.

Only the substitute.
Only the Lamb.
Only the One who stood where Barabbas should have stood.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
Imagine Barabbas stepping out into the light.

No chains.
No sentence.
No cross.

But somewhere behind him, Jesus is being beaten.
Mocked.
Spit on.
Crowned with thorns.
The freedom of Barabbas cost Jesus everything.
And your salvation is no different.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
Read that again.

He who knew no sin
was made sin for us.

That does not mean Jesus became sinful.
It means He bore the full legal guilt and punishment of sinners in their place.
The judgment fell on Him so grace could fall on us.

This is not sentimental religion.
This is holy substitution.
This is divine mercy without divine compromise.

God did not ignore sin.
He judged it fully—on the cross of Christ.
“Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” — 1 Peter 3:18
The just for the unjust.

Jesus for Barabbas.
Jesus for sinners.
Jesus for you.
So the question is not whether Barabbas was guilty.
The question is: what did Barabbas do with his freedom?
Scripture does not tell us.
And maybe that silence is intentional.
Because now the spotlight turns to you.

You have heard the Gospel.
You know the exchange.
You know who took the cross.
So what will you do with the freedom purchased by Another?

Will you go back to your rebellion?
Will you treat grace like permission?
Will you keep playing religious games while your heart stays hard?
Will you admire Jesus and still refuse to bow?
God saw it.
You knew.

There are many people who want a released-Barabbas life without a crucified-and-risen Christ as Lord. They want escape from consequences, but not repentance. They want comfort, but not surrender. They want heaven, but not holiness.
That is not salvation.
“Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” — Luke 13:3

Repentance is not perfection.
It is turning.
Turning from sin.
Turning from self-rule.
Turning to Jesus Christ in faith.

And faith is not merely believing facts.
It is trusting the Person who took your place.
“Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved…” — Acts 16:31
Saved from what?

From sin.
From wrath.
From judgment.
From yourself.
From the eternal consequences of rejecting the Son of God.
Because the story did not end with Jesus condemned.
They buried Him.
But death could not keep Him.
“He is not here: for he is risen, as he said…” — Matthew 28:6

The substitute did not stay in the grave.
The Lamb rose in victory.
The innocent One who died for sinners now reigns as Lord.
And that changes everything.
Because this is not just about a prisoner being released in Jerusalem long ago.
This is about heaven offering mercy to the guilty right now.

This is about your chains.
Your record.
Your secret sin.
Your coming judgment.
And this is about Christ standing in the middle and saying, in effect:
Let the guilty one go. I will take his place.
That is grace.

Undeserved.
Unbought.
Unimaginable.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
While we were yet sinners.

Not cleaned up.
Not improved.
Not worthy.
Sinners.

Barabbas-level guilty.
And still Christ died.

So stop pretending your sin is too small to matter.
And stop pretending your sin is too great for Christ to forgive.
Both lies keep people from the cross.
The truth is sharper.

Your sin is damnable.
Christ is sufficient.

Your guilt is real.
His blood is enough.

Your heart is corrupt.
His mercy is greater.

The Law says: guilty.
Grace says: Christ has paid.
But grace must be received through repentance and faith.
This is your moment of decision.

Not tomorrow.
Not when life settles down.
Not after one more secret indulgence.
Not after one more season of rebellion.
Now.

Come to Christ.
Bring your guilt.
Bring your shame.
Bring the record you cannot erase.
Bring the chains you pretend are not there.

Come broken.
Come honest.
Come empty.
But come.
Because the same Jesus who took the cross for the guilty also says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37
That means the door is open.

For the addict.
For the hypocrite.
For the sexual sinner.
For the bitter.
For the violent.
For the liar.
For the church actor.
For the rebel.
For the Barabbas in all of us.
But not on your terms.
On His.

Repent.
Believe.
Bow.
Follow.

And then do not just celebrate being released.
Follow the One who was pierced for your release.
This is where the Gospel Warrior message cuts through the noise: you are not saved to remain Barabbas. You are saved to become new in Christ.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17

That is discipleship.
That is transformation.
That is the evidence of grace.

Not perfection overnight.
But a new Master.
A new heart.
A new direction.
A new life under the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
So when you hear the name Barabbas, do not just think of an ancient criminal.
Think of the mirror.
Think of the exchange.
Think of the cross that should have been yours.
And then think of Jesus—bleeding, silent, holy, willing.
For you.

The guilty walked free.
The innocent was condemned.
Mercy opened the prison.
Love climbed the hill.
Grace took the nails.
And now the risen Christ stands before a world full of Barabbases and offers the same saving message:
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Before I end, hear this clearly: you are not the hero of this story. Barabbas was not the hero. The crowd was not the hero. Pilate was not the hero.
Jesus is the hero.

Jesus the substitute.
Jesus the sacrifice.
Jesus the risen King.
Jesus the only name by which sinners can be saved.
“Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.” — Acts 4:12
So choose this day.
Will you walk away unchanged like a man merely spared from death?
Or will you fall before the Christ who died and rose again to give you eternal life?

The prison door is open.
The cross is empty.
The tomb is vacant.
The invitation is real.
Come to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Ethiopian Eunuch: Inclusion in the Kingdom
paragraphs: The Ethiopian Eunuch: Inclusion in the Kingdom

He had power.
He had position.
He had access to wealth, influence, government, and prestige.
But he was still riding home empty.
That is the tragedy nobody sees.

You can sit close to power and still feel far from God.
You can travel to worship and still not know Him.
You can read holy words and still not understand the way of salvation.
That was the Ethiopian eunuch.

A man of authority.
A man of responsibility.
A man returning from Jerusalem.
A man reading Isaiah in his chariot.
And still... searching.
Acts 8:27–28 says:

“And behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,
Was returning, and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet.”
Read that again.

He had come to worship.
But worship attendance is not the same as new birth.
Religious activity is not the same as reconciliation with God.
That is where many people are right now.

You know the language.
You know the culture.
You know the songs.
You know when to bow your head and when to say “amen.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can be near sacred things and still be outside peace with God.

The eunuch carried a deeper tension than politics or status. In the ancient world, he would have known exclusion. He would have known what it meant to stand near, but not fully inside. He would have known the ache of distance. He had a scroll in his hands, but unanswered questions in his soul.
And God saw it.

Not just the chariot.
Not just the road.
Not just the scroll.
God saw the man.

This is the glory of the Gospel: God does not only summon the clean, the qualified, the insiders, the socially accepted, the ceremonially welcomed. He seeks the outsider. He pursues the one who has been marked, wounded, disqualified in the eyes of men.

Because the Kingdom of God is not built on human gatekeeping.
It is opened by Jesus Christ.
Acts 8:29–31 says:

“Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot.
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me?...”
That line is heavy.
“How can I...?”
He was reading truth without seeing the Person the truth was pointing to.

That is spiritual blindness.
And no amount of education, morality, or effort can heal it.

You do not need more self-improvement.
You need revelation.
You need Christ.
The eunuch was reading from Isaiah 53, the chapter soaked in blood, sorrow, substitution, and salvation.
Acts 8:32–33 says:

“He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth:
In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth.”

He was reading about suffering.
He was reading about rejection.
He was reading about a man crushed, humiliated, cut off.
And maybe that is why this mattered so deeply.

Because the broken can recognize brokenness.
The rejected can feel the weight of rejection.
The cut-off know what it means to be cut off.

But Isaiah 53 is not merely about pain.
It is about substitution.
Isaiah 53:5–6 says:

“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
There it is.

Not inspiration.
Not moral advice.
Not “do better.”

Sin.
Judgment.
A Substitute.
Grace.

Philip did not give him a motivational speech.
Philip did not tell him to believe in himself.
Philip did not tell him that all spiritual paths lead to God.
No.
Acts 8:35 says:
“Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.”
Jesus.

Not religion without blood.
Not ethics without atonement.
Not spirituality without repentance.
Jesus Christ.

This is the center of everything.
The eunuch was not saved by being sincere.
He was not saved by making a pilgrimage.
He was not saved by handling a scroll.
He was not saved by his status, his humility, or his curiosity.
He was confronted with Jesus.

The Son of God.
The Lamb of God.
The crucified Messiah.
The risen Lord.
The only name by which sinners are saved.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And this is where inclusion in the Kingdom becomes shocking.

Because the question is not: Are you impressive enough?
The question is not: Are you clean enough?
The question is not: Do people approve of you?
The question is: What have you done with Jesus Christ?

The Kingdom does not open because you finally become worthy.
The Kingdom opens because Christ was worthy in your place.
God had spoken of this long before.
Isaiah 56:3–5 says:

A place.
A name.
Within My walls.
Do you see it?

What law exposed, grace in Christ redeems.
What distance revealed, Jesus removes.
What exclusion symbolized, the Gospel overturns.

Not by pretending sin is small.
Not by erasing holiness.
But by satisfying justice at the cross.

That is the difference between human inclusion and Gospel inclusion.
The world includes by lowering standards.
God includes by fulfilling righteousness in His Son.
Read that again.

The cross is not God ignoring sin.
The cross is God punishing sin in Christ so sinners who repent and believe can be brought near.
Romans 3:23–24 says:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
All have sinned.

That includes the visibly broken and the publicly respected.
The religious and the rebellious.
The outsider and the insider.

You.
Me.
All.

God saw it.
You knew.

That hidden pride.
That secret lust.
That bitterness you keep feeding.
That image management.
That performance Christianity.
That private rebellion dressed in public respectability.
Spiritual diagnosis: your greatest problem is not exclusion by people, but separation from God because of sin.

And your greatest need is not affirmation.
It is redemption.

So when the eunuch heard Jesus preached, something happened.
Hope came alive.
Acts 8:36 says:
“And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?”
Listen to that cry.
What hinders me?

That is the cry of every soul that has lived under the shadow of distance.
Every person who thinks, Surely not me.
Every person who believes grace is for cleaner people, better people, less stained people.
What hinders me?
Philip’s answer strikes at the center.
Acts 8:37 says:
“And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”
There it is.

Not pedigree.
Not ceremony first.
Not works.
Faith in Jesus Christ.
That is the doorway into the Kingdom.

And yes, true faith produces obedience.
Yes, baptism matters.
Yes, repentance is real.
But the ground of salvation is Christ alone, received by faith.
The eunuch went down into the water not to earn entrance, but because he had found the King.
And when he came up, he did not leave with a theory.
He left with joy.
Acts 8:39 says:
“...he went on his way rejoicing.”
Rejoicing.

Because when Jesus saves a man, He does not merely adjust behavior.
He gives peace.
He gives adoption.
He gives belonging.
He gives a new name, a new future, a new heart.
This is inclusion in the Kingdom.

Not token acceptance.
Not sentimental tolerance.
Not emotional comfort without truth.
This is a blood-bought welcome for repentant sinners through Jesus Christ.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
And maybe this is your story too.

You know what it feels like to stand on the edge.
To carry shame.
To carry questions.
To carry the silent belief that everyone else gets in, but not you.
But here is the truth:
John 6:37
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
In no wise.

Not because your past is light.
Not because your record is clean.
Not because your wounds are imaginary.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.

So repent.
Turn from sin.
Stop hiding behind religion, excuses, intellect, pain, or delay.
Come to Christ.

The road to Gaza was deserted.
But Heaven was not absent there.
And the same God who sent Philip to a searching man still sends His Word today.

To the broken.
To the ashamed.
To the outsider.
To the religious but empty.
To the one whispering, What hinders me?

Nothing hinders you—
except unbelief.

Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ.
Trust the One who was wounded for transgressors.
Trust the Lamb who was slaughtered for sinners.
Trust the risen King who brings the far-off near.
Ephesians 2:13 says:
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.”

Far off.
Made near.
By the blood of Christ.

That is the Gospel.
That is the Kingdom.
That is your invitation.

Decision moment:
Will you keep reading about Him from a distance?
Or will you bow to Him as Lord?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Centurion: Faith Outside the “Chosen”
paragraphs: The Centurion: Faith Outside the “Chosen”
You thought being close to religion meant being close to God.
You thought knowing the language, carrying the label, standing near the temple, sitting near the truth, made you safe.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can grow up around the things of God and still miss God Himself.
And someone you would never expect can recognize Jesus faster than the people who were raised with the promises.
That is the shock of the centurion.

A Roman soldier.
An outsider.
A man outside the covenant people.
A man not born among the “chosen.”
A man with no tribal inheritance in Israel.
And yet when he met Jesus, he saw what many in Israel refused to see:
Authority. Mercy. Lordship.
Read that again.
The scandal in the street
In Matthew 8:5–10, a centurion comes to Jesus pleading for his servant:

“Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, dreadfully tormented.”
Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.”
The centurion answered and said, “Lord, I am not worthy that You should come under my roof. But only speak a word, and my servant will be healed…”
“When Jesus heard it, He marveled, and said to those who followed, ‘Assuredly, I say to you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel.’”
Not even in Israel.
Do you hear the weight of that?

The people with the Scriptures.
The people with the prophets.
The people with the covenants.
The people with the history.
And yet Jesus says this foreigner saw more clearly.
Why?
Because proximity to truth is not the same as surrender to truth.
Because heritage cannot replace repentance.
Because religion without faith is still unbelief.
The diagnosis nobody wants
You can be “chosen” in appearance and dead in heart.
You can know the stories and not know the Savior.
You can quote Scripture, defend doctrine, attend church, post verses, and still resist the authority of Jesus in the secret place.
God saw it.
You knew.

The centurion did not come with credentials.
He came with need.

He did not come demanding status.
He came confessing unworthiness.
“Lord, I am not worthy…”
That line alone exposes an entire generation trained to speak about God without trembling before Him.
The centurion understood two things many religious people still do not understand:

First, Jesus has absolute authority.
Second, he himself was absolutely undeserving.
That is where real faith begins.

Not with spiritual swagger.
With surrender.
Authority recognized by an outsider
The centurion says in essence: I know authority when I see it. I live under command, and I give commands. If You speak, sickness obeys.

He saw that Jesus did not merely pray for power.
Jesus carried power.

He did not see Jesus as a teacher only.
He saw Him as Lord.
This is the dividing line.

Many admire Jesus.
Few bow to Him.

Many want His compassion.
Few submit to His command.

Many want healing.
Few want holiness.
But the centurion saw both mercy and majesty in one Person.
That is faith.

Not vague spirituality.
Not emotional inspiration.
Not inherited tradition.
Faith is seeing Jesus rightly.
Law on one side. Grace on the other.
Israel had the Law. The covenants. The promises. The temple system.
“To them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.” — Romans 9:4
Yet privilege became presumption for many.
They assumed closeness to sacred things guaranteed peace with God.
But Scripture crushes that lie.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
All.

Jew and Gentile.
Religious and irreligious.
Insider and outsider.

The problem was never merely ethnicity.
The problem was sin.

And the answer was never mere lineage.
The answer was Christ.
“Therefore know that only those who are of faith are sons of Abraham.” — Galatians 3:7
Read that again.
Only those who are of faith.

Not performance.
Not ancestry.
Not reputation.
Not your family’s Christianity.
Not your ministry résumé.
Not your church attendance streak.
Faith.
And even that faith is not faith in yourself, but faith in Jesus Christ.
Jesus breaks the walls men build
Then Jesus says something even more explosive:

“And I say to you that many will come from east and west, and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into outer darkness.” — Matthew 8:11–12
This was not just a compliment to one soldier.
This was a warning shot to everyone trusting in spiritual entitlement.

Many from east and west.
Outsiders.
Far-off people.
Unexpected people.
People you wrote off.
People religion looked down on.
And some “sons of the kingdom” cast out.
Why?
Because being near the story is not the same as belonging to the King.
You can carry the badge and miss the banquet.
You can look like the insider and die as the stranger.
That should shake you.
The offense of grace
Religious pride hates this story.
Because grace does not move according to human ranking.
Grace humiliates the proud and welcomes the broken.

Grace does not ask, “Were you raised in the right atmosphere?”
Grace asks, “Do you believe the Son?”
“He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God…” — John 1:11–12
As many as received Him.
That means the door swings open far wider than proud religion wanted.
But it also means the door is narrower than human self-righteousness can tolerate.
Because the door is not heritage.
The door is Jesus.
“I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved…” — John 10:9

Not by bloodline.
Not by morality.
Not by nation.
Not by denomination.
By Me, Jesus says.
The centurion’s faith was not generic
This matters.
The centurion did not merely “believe in something.”
He believed Jesus could do what only God-authorized power could do.
His faith had an object.

Not positivity.
Not ritual.
Not sincerity by itself.
Jesus.
That is why salvation is not earned by being decent. It is received by grace through faith in Christ.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works…” — Ephesians 2:8–9
And this grace is necessary because sin is real.

Not mistakes.
Not flaws.
Not bad habits.
Sin.

Rebellion against a holy God.
Hidden filth.
Private compromise.
Open defiance.
Self-rule.
God saw it.
You knew.
And yet the same Christ who marveled at the centurion’s faith would go to the cross for sinners from every tribe and tongue.
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
That is the Gospel.

Not “try harder.”
Not “be more deserving.”
Not “earn your place among the chosen.”
The Gospel is this:

You are a sinner.
You cannot save yourself.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sin and rose again.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Receive mercy you did not earn.
Receive righteousness you could never produce.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
And here is where this turns from history into confrontation.
Because some of you are not the centurion.
You are the crowd.

Close enough to watch.
Too proud to kneel.

Some of you have been around church so long that the shock is gone.
The cross is familiar.
The words are familiar.
The songs are familiar.
But your heart is still untouched.
Others of you feel disqualified, too far gone, too outside, too stained, too foreign to grace.
This story crushes both lies.

To the proud insider, Jesus says:
Your status cannot save you.

To the broken outsider, Jesus says:
Come. Believe Me.
That is why the centurion matters.
He is living proof that faith can appear where religion least expects it.
He is a warning that spiritual privilege can rot into unbelief.
He is a signpost pointing beyond ethnicity, beyond ceremony, beyond human categories, straight to Christ.
The real chosen question
People keep asking, “Who are the chosen?”
But here’s the deeper question:
Have you come to the Chosen One?
Because all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ.
“For all the promises of God in Him are Yes, and in Him Amen…” — 2 Corinthians 1:20

Outside of Christ, heritage cannot save you.
Inside Christ, grace can redeem you.
The centurion stood outside the covenant nation, but he came to the covenant Lord.
And that changed everything.
Decision moment
So where are you in this story?
Are you the religious insider trusting your nearness to holy things?

Or are you the humbled sinner who says,
“Lord, I am not worthy… but speak a word”?

One posture is condemned.
The other is commended.

One clings to identity without repentance.
The other falls at Jesus’ feet.

One assumes.
The other believes.
Repent.

Turn from sin.
Turn from pride.
Turn from empty religion.
Turn from self-trust.
And believe in Jesus Christ.

Not merely as helper.
As Lord.

Not merely as example.
As Savior.

Not merely as a name in your content.
As the King with authority to forgive, cleanse, heal, and save.
Open loop for the soul
The scandal of the centurion is still happening.
People raised “inside” are walking away cold.
People once called “outside” are falling at the feet of Jesus in broken, trembling faith.
So do not trust the label.
Do not trust the crowd.
Do not trust your history.
Trust Christ.
And if a Roman centurion could recognize the glory of Jesus from outside the camp, what excuse will you give standing this close to the truth?
Read that again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Lazarus: Why Did Jesus Wait?
paragraphs: Lazarus: Why Did Jesus Wait?

Jesus was not late.
He was deliberate.
That is the part your pain struggles to believe.
Because when Lazarus got sick, Jesus did not rush. He did not sprint to Bethany. He did not send immediate relief. He did not heal him from a distance, though He had done that before. He waited.
And Lazarus died.
Read that again.

He waited.
And Lazarus died.

For the broken, that sounds cruel at first. Because you know what it feels like to pray and hear nothing. To beg God to move and watch the situation get worse. To ask for healing, rescue, restoration, and instead watch the door close, the body weaken, the relationship collapse, the opportunity rot in front of you.

You prayed.
God saw it.
You cried.
God saw it.
You thought He would come sooner.
You knew.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus sometimes delays what you want because He is preparing something greater than what you asked for.

In John 11:3–6, the sisters sent word to Jesus:
“Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.”
And after hearing it, Jesus said:
“This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby.”
Then Scripture says something shocking:
“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.”
Did you catch that?

Not although He loved them.
Because He loved them, He waited.
That destroys the lie that delay always means abandonment.

Sometimes the silence of God is not rejection.
Sometimes it is positioning.
Sometimes it is holy restraint.
Sometimes Jesus will let a situation pass the point of human fixing so that when He moves, no one can confuse His power with human effort.
That is where many of you are fighting God.

You do not just want His help.
You want His help on your schedule.
You want divine power, but under your terms.
You want resurrection without death.
Victory without surrender.
Glory without brokenness.
But that is not how Jesus works.

He does not merely improve dead things.
He raises them.
And before He raises them, He often lets everyone discover that they are truly dead.

That is not just Lazarus’ story.
That is yours.

Your sin was not “sickness” that needed a little moral treatment.
It was death.

Ephesians 2:1 says,
“And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.”

Dead. Not wounded.
Dead. Not struggling a little.
Dead in sin.
Separated from God.
Unable to save yourself.
Unable to clean yourself up enough for heaven.
That is the spiritual diagnosis.

You were not waiting for advice.
You were waiting for resurrection.
And that is why the Lazarus story is bigger than a funeral. It is a mirror.

Martha and Mary thought the crisis was sickness.
Jesus knew the deeper issue was revelation.

They wanted healing.
Jesus intended glory.

They wanted intervention before death.
Jesus planned to reveal Himself after death.
Because there is something about a sealed tomb that exposes what people truly believe.
When Jesus finally arrived, Martha met Him with the sentence many people still carry in their hearts:
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” — John 11:21
That is the cry of disappointed faith.
“Lord, if You had acted sooner…”

If You had answered that prayer sooner.
If You had saved that marriage sooner.
If You had stopped that addiction sooner.
If You had healed that body sooner.
If You had opened that door sooner.
That is where heartbreak becomes accusation.

But Jesus did not answer Martha with an apology.
He answered her with Himself.
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” — John 11:25

Not, “I know resurrection.”
Not, “I can teach on life.”
Not, “I can improve outcomes.”
“I am.”
This is the center.

Jesus did not come merely to solve one family’s tragedy.
He came to reveal that He is the only Lord over death, sin, judgment, and the grave.
And this is where the Gospel turns sharp.

Because many people want Jesus as comfort, but not as Lord.
As helper, but not as King.
As emotional support, but not as Savior from sin.
You want Him near enough to soothe you, but not holy enough to confront you.

But Jesus does not step into Bethany to offer sentimental words.
He steps in as the Son of God who commands the grave.
And before He speaks to Lazarus, He tells them something uncomfortable:
“Take ye away the stone.” — John 11:39

Martha resists:
“Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.”
There it is.
Exposure.

By now, it smells.
By now, it is undeniable.
By now, nobody can pretend it is not gone.

That is what many of you fear spiritually. You do not want the stone moved because you know what is behind it. Secret sin. Hypocrisy. pornography. pride. bitterness. unbelief. religious performance. hidden compromise. The image you protected. The rot you managed. The tomb you decorated.

God saw it.
You knew.
And still you hoped maybe Jesus would bless the outside without opening the inside.
He will not.
He loves too deeply to leave the stone in place.

Because grace is not denial.
Grace is resurrection truth breaking into the place you stopped hoping.
Then Jesus prays, lifts His eyes, and cries with a loud voice:
“Lazarus, come forth.” — John 11:43
And the dead man came out.

Bound hand and foot.
Face wrapped.
Alive, but still carrying grave clothes.
That is another word for somebody right now.
Jesus can bring you out of death in an instant, but sanctification is the process of taking off what belonged to your grave.

Saved, but still learning.
Alive, but still being unbound.
Free in Christ, but still shedding what your old life wrapped around you.
That is why salvation is not behavior modification. It is new life in Jesus Christ.
And how do you receive that life?

Not by works.
Not by trying harder.
Not by religious performance.
Not by pretending you are not dead.

Ephesians 2:8–9 says,
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.”
This is the Gospel:

You sinned against a holy God.
Your sin deserved judgment.
You could not save yourself.
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, lived without sin, died on the cross for sinners, and rose again in victory.
He took the punishment sin deserved.
He offers mercy, forgiveness, and eternal life to all who repent and believe.
That means the deepest reason Jesus waited at Lazarus’ tomb points beyond Bethany to Calvary.
Because soon, Jesus Himself would be laid in a tomb.
But unlike Lazarus, Jesus did not die because sickness touched Him. He died because He willingly took the place of sinners. And unlike Lazarus, Jesus rose never to die again.

Lazarus was a sign.
Jesus is the Savior.

Lazarus came out still needing others to loose him.
Jesus rose in total triumph, having crushed death itself.

Romans 5:8 says,
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”

And 1 Corinthians 15:55–57 declares,
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? ... thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
So why did Jesus wait?

He waited to reveal that His love is deeper than immediate relief.
He waited to reveal that faith must rest in who He is, not only in what He does.
He waited to reveal that when human hope is buried, divine glory can still speak.
He waited to show that He is not merely a healer of the sick, but the resurrection of the dead.
And maybe that is why He has allowed certain things in your life to reach the point where your strength failed.

Not because He is absent.
Not because He is powerless.
Not because He is cruel.

But because He is bringing you to the end of yourself, where you stop trusting your ability, your goodness, your religion, your excuses, and finally fall before the only One who can call dead things to live.
This is your decision moment.

Stop accusing God for not serving your timeline.
Stop dressing up a tomb and calling it life.
Stop hiding behind delay as an excuse for unbelief.
Repent.

Turn from sin.
Turn from self.
Turn from dead religion.
Turn to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest miracle in the Lazarus story is not that one man came out of a tomb.
It is that the same Christ still speaks life to the spiritually dead.

And when He calls, you do not negotiate.
You come out.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
But Jesus is still writing stories where graves become testimonies.

So hear the voice behind the tears.
Hear the authority behind the silence.
Hear the Christ who waited, not to destroy hope, but to redefine it.

The tomb is not bigger than Jesus.
Your sin is not deeper than His mercy.
Your delay is not stronger than His purpose.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

The question was never only, “Why did Jesus wait?”
The real question is:
When He calls your name, will you come out?
Read that again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lessons I Learned from Vashti
paragraphs: The Lessons I Learned from Vashti
Most people read Vashti and move on.
A queen. A refusal. A removal. End of story.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God can use even a brief, painful moment in someone’s life to expose pride, shift kingdoms, and prepare the stage for something far bigger than human power. Read that again.

Vashti appears in only a small portion of Scripture, but her story in Esther 1 still speaks. Not because she is the center. Jesus is always the center. But because her moment reveals something about dignity, power, consequence, and the fragile glory of this world.
And that matters for you.

This is the kind of Bible reflection Gospel Warrior returns to often—because hidden in these short passages are deep confrontations for the soul. For more Christ-centered teachings and deeper discipleship resources, visit Gospel Warrior and keep growing here:
1. Earthly crowns can disappear in a moment
Vashti was queen.
She had status, influence, recognition, and a place in the palace. But one royal command, one public refusal, and her position was gone. That is how fragile earthly glory is.
Titles look strong until they are tested. Platforms look secure until God allows one moment to reveal how temporary they really are.
You can be admired today and forgotten tomorrow. Celebrated in one room and replaced in the next.
That is not just Vashti’s lesson. That is ours.
If your identity is built on beauty, applause, position, marriage, success, or public approval, it is standing on sand. This world rewards you for a season, then moves on without mercy.
But here is the deeper issue: sin trains the human heart to trust temporary crowns more than the eternal King.
And that is why we need Jesus.
Because Christ does not offer borrowed glory. He gives redemption. He gives a kingdom that cannot be shaken. He gives an identity not rooted in performance, but in grace.
2. Not every act of defiance is automatically righteousness
This is where we must be careful.
Scripture tells us Vashti refused the king’s command. It does not tell us every motive in her heart. So we should not force the text to say more than God said.
Some people turn Vashti into a symbol of pure courage. Others reduce her to rebellion. The honest answer is this: the text does not fully explain her inner motive.
Read that again.
And there is a lesson in that too.
We live in a generation that loves quick heroes and quick villains. But Scripture teaches us to slow down, humble ourselves, and let God’s Word speak with precision.

Still, one thing is certain: the palace was full of pride, drunkenness, vanity, and misuse of authority. The entire scene in Esther 1 is soaked in human arrogance. Vashti’s story unfolds inside a corrupt environment.
That means this chapter is not ultimately about female strength, male weakness, court politics, or social commentary.
It is about the bankruptcy of human rule without God.

Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this reminder matters now more than ever: whenever sin rules the room, everyone in it is affected. The proud command. The fearful advise. The powerful manipulate. The vulnerable suffer.
That is what sin does.
And that is why behavior modification is never enough. We do not just need better decisions. We need a new heart.
3. God is working even when His name is not mentioned
The book of Esther is famous for this.
God’s name is not explicitly mentioned, yet His hand is everywhere.
Vashti is removed. Esther is eventually positioned. A crisis is coming. Deliverance is being prepared before anyone in the palace can see it.
That should encourage you.

Because some of the most important moments in your life will feel hidden, confusing, unfair, and unresolved. You will not always see the hand of God clearly while you are living inside the tension of the story.
But His silence is not His absence.

He is still sovereign over closed doors. Sovereign over unjust systems. Sovereign over losses you did not plan. Sovereign over moments that feel like endings but are really transitions in His larger purpose.
This post is only the surface. The deeper equipping is there for those who are ready to keep walking:
4. Human empires are loud, but God’s providence is stronger
Esther 1 is full of spectacle.
Royal garments. Wealth. wine. Decrees. Public image. Political panic.
It is theatrical.
And yet all that noise cannot stop the quiet providence of God.

This is one of the strongest lessons I learned from Vashti’s story: men make decrees, but God directs history. Kings react emotionally, but God moves intentionally. Empires protect image, but God preserves His people.
That should break the intimidation off your life.
The world still loves appearances. It still worships power. It still writes laws, creates narratives, rewards compromise, and punishes disruption. But none of that overrules heaven.
Jesus Christ is not threatened by the rise of earthly systems. He is Lord over all.
So do not fear the palace more than you fear God. Do not chase acceptance from people who are themselves passing away. Do not build your life around rooms that heaven never anointed.
5. A hidden lesson in Vashti’s story is the danger of pride on every side
King Ahasuerus was proud. His empire was proud. His banquet was proud. His advisors were proud.
But pride is not only a throne problem.
It is a heart problem.

Pride can live in rulers, and pride can live in the wounded. Pride can live in the celebrated, and pride can live in the rejected. Pride can speak loudly, and pride can also sit silently inside self-protection.
That is why the lesson of Vashti cannot stop at palace politics.
It has to come to you.
Where is pride ruling in your life?

Where do you resist God’s authority while criticizing someone else’s misuse of authority? Where have you built your identity on being right, seen, admired, chosen, or vindicated? Where are you still wearing a crown in your mind that God is trying to remove for your salvation?
This is the breaking point.
Because until sin is named, grace is treated like decoration.
And sin is not merely “bad choices.” Sin is rebellion against a holy God. Sin distorts our desires, blinds our judgment, corrupts power, and leaves every one of us in need of mercy.
Not advice.
Mercy.
6. Jesus is the better King every broken story is crying out for
This is where the story turns.
Vashti’s account shows us the failure of human authority. Esther will later show courage and providence. But the whole Bible is moving toward Someone greater.
Jesus is the true and righteous King no earthly ruler could ever be.

He does not exploit for display. He lays down His life in love.
He does not rule through drunken pride. He reigns in holiness.
He does not discard sinners who come to Him broken. He redeems them by grace.
That is the Gospel.

You and I are sinners. We have lived under the corruption of pride, fear, rebellion, self-rule, and misplaced worship. We deserve judgment, not applause. But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again, so that all who repent and believe in Him can be forgiven, cleansed, and made new.
This is not self-improvement.
This is redemption.
Not by works. Not by image management. Not by religious effort. By grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone.
If this found you, it’s not by accident.
The lesson of Vashti is not merely “stand up for yourself,” or “be careful with power,” or “life changes fast.” Those may brush the surface.
The deepest lesson is this: every human kingdom is unstable, every human heart is corrupted by sin, and every human story desperately needs the intervention of God.
And in Jesus, that intervention has come.
7. What I learned from Vashti, personally
I learned not to worship temporary crowns.
I learned to be careful with conclusions when Scripture is brief.
I learned that God is moving even in chapters where His hand seems hidden.
I learned that pride can destroy a palace and poison a soul.
And above all, I learned that no earthly king can do for me what Jesus has already done through the cross and resurrection.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can know all those lessons and still miss the point if they do not lead you to repentance and faith in Christ.
So let this be more than reflection. Let it be surrender.
Follow the source. Stay rooted in Scripture. Go deeper than quotes and surface inspiration. Gospel Warrior exists to point people to Jesus Christ with clarity, conviction, and truth.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Abner
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Abner
Most people read past Abner.

He is rarely the sermon title. Rarely the poster. Rarely the man anyone stops for.
Not David. Not Saul. Not Samuel. Not even Joab.
Abner feels like background.

But here’s what most people don’t realize: some of the most dangerous people in Scripture are not always the loudest rebels. Sometimes they are the powerful men standing close to the truth… while never fully surrendering to it.
And that is why Abner matters.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is one of those overlooked biblical portraits that exposes the heart with uncomfortable precision.
Abner was strong. Influential. Respected. Political. Necessary.

He was “the commander of Saul’s army” (1 Samuel 14:50), a man of rank, proximity, and military weight. He stood near the throne. He knew the movements of kings. He understood power. He could shape outcomes.
But being near the kingdom is not the same as belonging to the King.
Read that again.

Abner spent much of his life defending a house God had already rejected. Scripture says, “Now the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul” (1 Samuel 16:14). That should stop you. Because Abner kept lending his strength to a collapsing kingdom, fighting to preserve what God had already judged.
How many people are doing that right now?

Still defending what God has left.
Still protecting what God has exposed.
Still building on pride, reputation, control, lust, ego, and self-rule—while calling it wisdom.

The tragedy of Abner is not that he lacked intelligence.
The tragedy is that he used his gifts to uphold the wrong throne.
Second Samuel says, “There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1).
That verse is bigger than politics. It is spiritual.

Anything built against God’s chosen King will weaken, no matter how impressive it looks at first. That includes human pride. That includes religious performance. That includes the version of you that wants blessings without surrender.
And this is where the story gets even heavier.

Abner knew David was rising. He was not blind. In fact, later he confessed what had long been obvious: “The Lord has promised David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel’” (2 Samuel 3:18).
He knew.

He knew what God had said.
He knew who God had chosen.
He knew where history was going.
But knowledge alone does not save anyone.

You can know truth and still resist it.
You can quote Scripture and still protect self.
You can recognize God’s hand and still delay obedience.
That delay is deadly.

Because Abner did not move toward David out of pure worship or broken repentance at first. He moved after offense, conflict, and wounded pride. When Ish-bosheth challenged him, Abner’s anger flared, and then he decided to transfer his loyalty (2 Samuel 3:6–10). That is sobering. He changed direction, yes—but not from a clean heart.

A lot of people turn only when ego gets bruised.
Not because sin is hated.
Not because God is holy.
Not because Christ is beautiful.
But because their idol stopped paying them back.
And still—this is where the Bible becomes terrifyingly honest and breathtakingly merciful—God’s purposes keep moving.

Even through damaged motives.
Even through compromised men.
Even through the ruins of ambition.
But do not miss the warning: influence without surrender is not faithfulness.

Abner had access. He had strength. He had strategic value. He could negotiate kingdoms. Yet for all his importance, he remains a picture of a man who stood close to God’s unfolding plan without being remembered as a model of wholehearted devotion.
That should shake every churchgoer who confuses involvement with obedience.

You can serve around holy things and still have an unsurrendered heart.
You can stand near David and miss the deeper need for redemption.
You can talk kingdom language while still being ruled by self.
And self-rule is the ancient poison.

Scripture does not flatter us. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Not some. All. The polished and the broken. The public sinner and the hidden manipulator. The rebel in the street and the respectable man in the war room.
Sin is not merely failure. It is rebellion against God. It is the enthronement of self.
That is why Abner’s story is not just about Abner.

It is about you.
It is about me.
It is about every heart that knows enough to be accountable but resists full surrender.
But here is where the story must turn—because the Bible never leaves the broken soul with diagnosis alone.
David, for all his significance, was never the final answer. He points forward. Beyond the battlefield. Beyond the throne of Israel. Beyond the political tension of 2 Samuel.
He points to Jesus Christ, the true and better King.

The Son of David.
The rejected King who is still God’s chosen King.
The One many overlook until it is too late.

John writes, “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). Like David in his rise, Jesus was resisted by those clinging to threatened kingdoms. Yet unlike every earthly king, Jesus came not merely to claim a throne but to save sinners.
And this is the heart of the Gospel.

We have all sided with the wrong kingdom.
We have all loved self more than God.
We have all sinned.
We deserve judgment.
“The wages of sin is death,” Romans 6:23 says, “but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Read that again.

Death is earned.
Grace is given.
And eternal life is not found in your effort, morality, family background, church activity, or biblical literacy. It is found in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Jesus lived the righteous life we failed to live. He died the death our sins deserved. “But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Then He rose again in victory, proving sin, death, and hell do not get the final word.

So the call is not, “Try harder.”
The call is not, “Become more impressive.”
The call is not, “Use your influence better so God will accept you.”
The call is: repent and believe the Gospel.
Scripture says, “Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19). And again: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31).
That is the line Abner’s story presses on your soul.

Will you keep strengthening the house God has rejected—your pride, your secret sin, your image, your self-made identity?
Or will you bow before the true King?
If this found you, it’s not by accident.

Maybe you have been near truth for years.
Maybe you know the verses.
Maybe you can identify the kingdom language.
Maybe, like Abner, you recognized God’s direction long ago but have not fully yielded.

Do not mistake delayed movement for obedience.
Do not confuse awareness with repentance.
Do not stand near the kingdom while resisting the King.
Jesus Christ is the only answer.
And here is the mercy that still stands open tonight:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Not partially.
Not reluctantly.
Not after you fix yourself.
By grace. Through faith. In Jesus Christ alone.

So do not just admire the lesson in Abner.
Let it confront you.
Let it expose you.
Let it drive you to the cross.
Because the overlooked character is revealing the overlooked danger: a heart close to the story of God, but not yet surrendered to the Son of God.
And that can change right now.

Call on Jesus. Turn from sin. Trust the crucified and risen Christ. Follow the source, not the counterfeit. And if you want to go deeper, Gospel Warrior is building a growing library for believers who are done playing games with lukewarm faith and ready to be equipped in truth:

title: Abraham: Faithful or Willing to Sacrifice Too Much?
paragraphs: Abraham: Faithful or Willing to Sacrifice Too Much?
Most people ask the question too late.

They wait until Isaac is on the altar.
They wait until the knife is lifted.
They wait until the moment feels unbearable.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

The story of Abraham in Genesis 22 is not mainly about a reckless father who loved religion more than his son. It is about a man who had learned, through fire and failure, that God is never cruel, never late, and never wrong. And if this found you, it’s not by accident.
Still, the tension should disturb you. It is supposed to.

God said, “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love… and offer him there as a burnt offering” (Genesis 22:2). Read that again. Whom you love. Scripture does not soften the weight. God names the wound before He tests the faith.

So was Abraham faithful?
Yes.

Was the moment terrifying?
Also yes.
And that is exactly why this story still grips the soul.

Abraham was not a perfect man. Before Mount Moriah, he had already stumbled in fear, deception, and impatience. He lied about Sarah. He tried to secure God’s promise through human effort with Hagar. This is not the story of a flawless hero. This is the story of a sinner being taught to trust the God of grace. Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is where shallow readings collapse: Abraham’s obedience was not blind fanaticism. It was forged in relationship, covenant, and revelation.
Now the real issue emerges.

Did Abraham love God more than Isaac?
Yes.
Should he have?
Yes again.

Jesus later says, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). That sounds severe until you understand who God is. God is not a rival to proper love. He is the source of it. When we put anyone above Him—even good gifts, even promised blessings—we turn love into idolatry.
That is what Genesis 22 exposes.

Isaac was not just Abraham’s son. Isaac was the promise. The future. The covenant line. The laughter after years of barren silence. To place Isaac on the altar was to place Abraham’s deepest earthly attachment before God and say, “Even this does not belong above You.”
But do not miss the deeper layer.

Hebrews tells us what Abraham believed: “He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead” (Hebrews 11:19). Abraham was not surrendering Isaac because he thought God delights in destruction. Abraham obeyed because he believed God could still keep His word even through death itself. That changes everything.
Read that again.

This was not faith in sacrifice.
This was faith in resurrection power before resurrection was fully revealed.

So no, Abraham was not “willing to sacrifice too much” in the sinful sense of abandoning all discernment for religious extremism. He was surrendering everything to the God who had already proven Himself trustworthy. That is a different category entirely.
And yet… the question still reaches into your life.
What is your Isaac?
What are you clinging to so tightly that obedience to God feels like loss? A relationship? A dream? A calling? A reputation? Your own plan for how the promise should unfold?
Sometimes the greatest idol in your life is not something evil. It is something God-given that you refuse to place back into God’s hands.
That is where sin hides in respectable clothes.

“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Not just the openly rebellious. Not just the immoral. Even the religious heart can cherish the gift more than the Giver. Even devotion can be mixed with self-preservation. Even faith can be infected with control.
And that is where the story turns from Abraham to you.

Because the breaking point is never only about the altar.
It is about the heart on the altar.
But here is where the gospel explodes into the scene.

At the decisive moment, God stops Abraham: “Do not lay your hand on the boy” (Genesis 22:12). Then Abraham lifts his eyes and sees a ram caught in a thicket. A substitute. A sacrifice provided by God Himself.
Do you see it?
Mount Moriah whispers the name of Jesus long before Bethlehem.

Abraham did not ultimately lose his son because one day God the Father would not spare His own. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Isaac walked down the mountain alive because centuries later Jesus would carry the wood of His own sacrifice and be led to the cross for sinners.

This is why the story cannot be reduced to moralism.
It is not, “Try harder to be like Abraham.”
It is, “Behold the God who provides.”

John the Baptist saw Jesus and declared, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Abraham named the place “The Lord will provide” (Genesis 22:14). In Christ, He has.

Your sin deserves judgment.
Your self-rule deserves death.
Your idols cannot save you.
But Jesus came for the guilty.

“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
“In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7).
That is the center. Not Abraham’s knife. Christ’s cross.
So was Abraham faithful?
Yes—because real faith trusts God even when obedience hurts.
Was he willing to sacrifice too much?

Not in the way critics mean. The real scandal is not that Abraham almost gave up his son. The real scandal is that God actually gave His Son for enemies like us. And unlike Isaac, Jesus was not spared, so that repentant sinners could be.

That means the call now is not admiration.
It is repentance.

Turn from sin.
Turn from idols.
Turn from self-made righteousness.
Turn to Jesus Christ alone.

“If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). Salvation is not earned by sacrifice. It is received by grace through faith. “For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
So yes, Abraham was faithful. But the greater point is this: faith does not end at Abraham. Faith must bring you to Christ.
And if this message stirred something in you, follow the source, not the noise. Gospel Warrior exists to bring people back to Scripture, back to the cross, and back to the King.
Before you move on, answer honestly:

What is the Isaac on your altar?
What are you afraid to surrender to God?
And do you trust the Father who provided the Lamb?
For those with eyes to see, the story was never about a father who loved too much or too little.

It was about the God who stops the knife for Isaac…
and does not stop the cross for Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Stephen: The Cost of Bold Truth
paragraphs: Stephen: The Cost of Bold Truth
They did not hate Stephen because he was weak.
They hated him because he would not bend.
He spoke with a face full of heaven and a mouth full of truth. And truth, when it confronts a hardened heart, does not get politely dismissed. It gets resisted. Mocked. Silenced. Sometimes violently.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Stephen’s story is not just about how a man died.
It is about what kind of faith is worth dying for.
And that question reaches straight into you.
Because many people say they love Jesus—until truth costs them something.
Until obedience costs reputation.
Until holiness costs relationships.
Until the Gospel costs comfort.
Then suddenly silence feels safer than faithfulness.
But Stephen did not choose safety.
He chose truth.
And truth had a price.
Stephen first appears as a servant, not a celebrity.
Acts 6 says he was “full of faith and of the Holy Spirit” and “full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people” (Acts 6:5, 8).
Read that again.
He was not famous because he chased influence.
He was powerful because he was full of God.
That is the difference.
This generation is full of noise, branding, image management, performance, religious theater.
Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit.
And when a man is full of the Spirit, he cannot stay empty in the face of compromise.
So opposition came.
Of course it did.
Scripture says, “They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking” (Acts 6:10).
They could not defeat the truth, so they twisted it.
That is still how darkness works.
If it cannot refute righteousness, it will slander it.
If it cannot silence heaven with logic, it will stir hatred with lies.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You told the truth, and they called you divisive.
You stood for Christ, and they called you extreme.
You refused to celebrate sin, and they called you hateful.
God saw it.
You knew.
The pressure was not just social. It was spiritual.
Then Stephen stood before the council.
He could have softened the edge.
He could have trimmed the message.
He could have made it more acceptable.
Instead, he preached.
Not self-help.
Not vague spirituality.
Truth.
He walked through Israel’s history and exposed a terrifying pattern: people claiming to honor God while resisting the very messengers God sent.
Then he struck the nerve.
“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).
That is not motivational language.
That is diagnosis.
And some of you need that same diagnosis.
You are not confused.
You are resisting.
You are not merely struggling.
You are stiff-necked in the places where God has already spoken.
You heard the conviction.
You felt the warning.
You knew the relationship was sinful.
You knew the habit was chains.
You knew the bitterness was poisoning you.
You knew the double life was killing your soul.
God saw it.
And still you kept going.
That is what sin does. It hardens. It blinds. It convinces people that delaying repentance is the same as escaping judgment.
It is not.
Stephen’s boldness did not come from arrogance.
It came from revelation.
Because as stones were being lifted, heaven opened.

Acts 7:55–56 says, “But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. And he said, ‘Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.’”
Jesus standing.
Not distant.
Not indifferent.
Standing.
As if heaven itself rose to receive a faithful witness.
Let that settle into your spirit.
The world may reject the one who stands for Christ.
But Christ does not reject the one who stands for Him.
This is the contrast most people miss:
The council was full of rage.
Stephen was full of glory.
They were losing control.
Stephen was seeing eternity.
They were clenching stones.
Stephen was beholding Jesus.
That is the dividing line between the flesh and the Spirit.
One side burns with hatred.
The other shines with heaven.
Then came the cost.
They dragged him out.
They stoned him.
And in that brutal moment, Stephen looked like his Savior.

“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
“Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59–60).
Where did that kind of mercy come from?
From the cross.
Because nobody forgives like that unless grace has already conquered them.
This is the Gospel at the center of Stephen’s death:

Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, was rejected, mocked, condemned, and crucified for sinners. He bore the wrath we deserved. He died in our place. He rose again in victory. And now forgiveness is offered—not to the righteous, not to the polished, not to the religious performers—but to sinners who repent and believe.
Stephen was not saved by courage.
He was saved by Christ.
His boldness was not the basis of his acceptance.
Jesus was.
That matters.
Because some of you hear a message like this and immediately think, “I need to try harder. Be braver. Do better.”
No.
You need more than moral resolve.
You need resurrection life.
You need your sins forgiven.
You need a new heart.
You need Jesus.
Law exposes.
Grace transforms.

The Law says, you are guilty.
The Gospel says, Christ has paid.
The Law says, you have fallen short.
The Gospel says, “by grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8).
The Law says, judgment is deserved.
The Gospel says, “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
Read that again.
Stephen’s story is not calling you to admire bravery from a distance.
It is calling you to decide.
Will you keep editing the truth to protect your comfort?
Will you keep muting conviction because repentance feels expensive?
Will you keep pretending neutrality is harmless?
There is a cost to bold truth.
Yes.
But there is a greater cost to rejecting it.
Stephen lost his life.
But those who killed him were in danger of losing their souls.
One man saw Jesus.
The others only saw the man they wanted removed.
That is the difference between spiritual sight and spiritual death.

And here is the mercy of God: even in Stephen’s execution, the Gospel kept moving. A young man named Saul was there. Watching. Approving. And later, the grace of Jesus would crush his rebellion and turn him into Paul.
So do not tell me God cannot save the hostile.
Do not tell me the resistant are too far gone.
Do not tell me the mocker is unreachable.
Grace still hunts persecutors.
Grace still breaks proud men.
Grace still turns enemies into preachers.
That means there is hope for you too.
Repent.
Turn from sin.
Turn from dead religion.
Turn from self-justification.
Turn to Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, reigning.
Because bold truth is costly.
But rejecting Christ costs everything.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Nehushtan: A Lesson in Godly Purity
paragraphs: Nehushtan: A Lesson in Godly Purity
There are things people keep long after God has moved on.

Not because those things are holy.
Because those things are familiar.
That was the tragedy of Nehushtan.

What once served as a sign of God’s mercy became an object of false worship. What once pointed beyond itself became the very thing people bowed to. And that is how impurity often enters a life—not always through obvious rebellion, but through misplaced reverence.

But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Idolatry does not always begin with evil things. Sometimes it begins with gifted things, sacred memories, spiritual experiences, or symbols God once used. Read that again.
In Numbers 21, when Israel sinned against the Lord, fiery serpents came among the people. Death spread through the camp. Then God, in mercy, gave Moses a strange instruction:

“And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.”
— Numbers 21:8
And Scripture says:

“And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.”
— Numbers 21:9

The bronze serpent was never the Savior.
It was a sign.

It was never the source of healing.
It was an instrument through which God chose to show mercy.
And for a time, it served its purpose.

But generations later, the people of Judah did something deadly. They took what God had once used and turned it into something God never commanded them to worship. In the days of King Hezekiah, Scripture says:

“He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.”
— 2 Kings 18:4

That word—Nehushtan—carries the idea of a mere piece of bronze.
Hezekiah stripped away the illusion. He exposed the lie. He called it what it really was.

Not revival.
Not glory.
Not God.
Just bronze.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is where the knife turns inward: how many people today are still burning incense to “Nehushtan”?
Not literally, perhaps. But spiritually? Constantly.

Some worship the memory of a past move of God.
Some worship church tradition more than Christ.
Some worship platforms, preachers, methods, relics, titles, aesthetics, family heritage, or emotional experiences.
Some are devoted to what once helped them encounter truth, but they no longer bow before the living God Himself.
And the Lord is not indifferent to that.

“Thou shalt have no other gods before me.”
— Exodus 20:3

“Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.”
— 1 John 5:21

Godly purity is not merely avoiding immoral behavior. It is the cleansing of worship. It is the tearing down of everything that competes with the throne of God in the heart. That is why this matters so deeply. Purity is not just about what you stop doing. It is about who alone you bow to.

Here is the deeper danger: religious corruption can look reverent on the outside. Burning incense looked spiritual. It looked sacred. It even involved something connected to biblical history. But sincerity does not sanctify disobedience.

“This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.”
— Matthew 15:8

That is the crisis of Nehushtan.
The form remained.
The fear of God did not.
And maybe that is where some souls are right now.

You still carry the symbol.
You still know the language.
You still preserve the memory.
But the fire of true devotion has been replaced by ritual, nostalgia, or attachment to what God used yesterday.
If this found you, it’s not by accident.
Because the lesson of Nehushtan is not just destruction. It is purification.

King Hezekiah did not negotiate with the idol.
He did not store it in a museum.
He did not rename it and keep it nearby.
He broke it.
That is what repentance does.

“Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.”
— Isaiah 55:7

Repentance is not sentimental.
It is violent against sin.
It is honest about substitutes.
It tears down what steals affection from God.
And this is where the Gospel shines brighter than the brass serpent ever could.
Jesus Himself took that image from Numbers and revealed its ultimate meaning:

“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
— John 3:14–15

The bronze serpent pointed forward to Christ.
Nehushtan was a corrupted sign.
Jesus is the spotless Savior.

Where Israel looked and lived physically, sinners now look to Christ and live eternally.
Where idols enslave, Jesus redeems.
Where religion corrupts, Jesus cleanses.
Where sin condemns, Jesus saves.
Because the real problem is deeper than misplaced symbols. The real problem is the sinful heart.

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
— Romans 6:23
That is why godly purity cannot be achieved by self-effort alone. You do not become clean by smashing one idol while secretly enthroning yourself. You need more than reform. You need redemption.
You need the blood of Jesus.

“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8

“In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.”
— Colossians 1:14

This is the call: repent of sin, turn from idols, and trust fully in Jesus Christ. Not in objects. Not in tradition. Not in religious performance. Not in your own strength. Salvation is by grace through faith.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.”
— Ephesians 2:8–9

So ask yourself plainly:
What has become Nehushtan in your life?

What are you protecting that God is calling you to break?
What are you revering that no longer points you to Christ?
What sacred-looking thing has quietly stolen the worship that belongs to God alone?
Read that again.
And here is the mercy of God: when He exposes the idol, He is not trying to ruin you. He is trying to free you.

“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
— John 8:36
Follow the source.
Bring every idol into the light. Turn to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’ve heard her name before—but not the way Scripture actually tells it.
paragraphs: You’ve heard her name before—but not the way Scripture actually tells it.
Bathsheba.
And almost every time she’s mentioned, there’s an unspoken accusation attached to her. Seductress. Opportunist. The woman who took a king down.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The Bible never calls her any of those things.
It never even hints at it.
What it does show—if you slow down enough to see it—is something far heavier. Something uncomfortable.
A woman with no power… caught in the path of a king who took what he wanted.
And God saw it.
The story begins in 2 Samuel 11, but not the way people often retell it. It opens with a quiet indictment—not of Bathsheba, but of David.
“In the spring, at the time when kings go out to battle… David remained at Jerusalem.” (2 Samuel 11:1)
He wasn’t where he was supposed to be.
You knew.
That detail matters, because everything that follows flows from a king out of position.
Then comes the moment everyone misinterprets.
David sees a woman bathing.
The Hebrew text says: “וַיַּרְא אִשָּׁה רֹחֶצֶת” (vayar ishah rochetzet)—“he saw a woman bathing.”
There is no seduction language. No flirtation. No invitation.
Just observation.
Then Scripture adds: “the woman was very beautiful to look upon.”
That description is from David’s perspective.
Not hers.
Read that again.
Then the shift happens.
David doesn’t approach her.
He sends for her.
The Hebrew verb used is “וַיִּקָּחֶהָ” (vayiqacheha)—“he took her.”
The same verb is used elsewhere in Scripture for taking something by authority, even force.
Not “she came to him willingly.”
Not “she enticed him.”
He took her.
And in the ancient Near Eastern context, a king’s summons was not a request you could decline. Refusal could mean death—not just for her, but for her family.
So when the text says, “she came to him,” it doesn’t describe desire.
It describes compliance under power.
Then comes the silence that people misjudge.
“She came to him, and he lay with her.” (2 Samuel 11:4)
No recorded dialogue.
No protest.
No resistance.
And people read that silence as consent.
But Scripture often records trauma without commentary.
Silence in the text does not equal agreement in reality.
It often reflects what victims cannot safely say.
And then, just one sentence from her:
“I am pregnant.”
That’s it.
No manipulation. No demand. No strategy.
Just consequence.
Now watch what happens next.
David panics.
He schemes.
He manipulates.
He orchestrates the death of her husband, Uriah.
And the Hebrew makes this chillingly clear.
In 2 Samuel 11:17, it says Uriah was struck down because David placed him where the fighting was fiercest.
That’s premeditated.
And Bathsheba?
Still silent in the narrative.
Because she has no control over any of it.
But God breaks the silence.
Through the prophet Nathan in 2 Samuel 12.
And notice who God condemns.
Not Bathsheba.
David.
“You struck down Uriah… and took his wife to be your wife.” (2 Samuel 12:9)
Again that word.
“Took.”
The Hebrew: לָקַח (laqach).
God Himself defines the act—not as mutual sin—but as an abuse of power.
And here’s something most people miss entirely.
When the child dies, Scripture says:
“David comforted Bathsheba his wife.” (2 Samuel 12:24)
Comfort.
Why would she need comfort?
Because she’s grieving.
Because she’s been through something devastating.
Because she’s not the villain people made her out to be.
Then something even deeper happens.
She gives birth again.
And this time, the child is named Solomon.
And Scripture says:
“The LORD loved him.” (2 Samuel 12:24)
God’s favor rests on the child of the same woman people still slander.
And it doesn’t stop there.
Bathsheba later appears in 1 Kings 1, advocating for Solomon’s rightful place—not as a manipulator, but as a mother navigating royal politics where survival required wisdom.
By this point, she has grown into influence—but that came later.
Not at the beginning.
Not that night.
Now go to the New Testament.
Matthew 1:6.
The genealogy of Jesus.
And it says:
“David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah.”
Not even named.
Still identified by what was done to her.
And yet…
She is in the lineage of Christ.
Let that sit.
The Greek here uses “ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου” (ek tēs tou Ouriou)—“from the [wife] of Uriah.”
It deliberately keeps the memory of injustice visible.
God does not erase what happened to her.
He redeems through it.
So why has she been misjudged for so long?
