Saul stood in the dark with a crown on his head and terror in his bones.
The Philistines were coming.
And God was silent.
“When Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.” — 1 Samuel 28:6
Read that again.
A man can wear the crown and still lose the presence.

Saul knew the law.
Saul knew witchcraft was forbidden.
Saul had once removed mediums from the land.
But fear has a way of making hypocrites run back to what they once condemned.
So Saul disguised himself.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
He wasn’t just hiding from people.
He was trying to hide from God.
God saw it.
You knew.
In the night, Saul went to Endor and asked a medium to summon Samuel.
The same Saul who refused obedience now wanted spiritual answers.
But delayed desperation is not repentance.
“To obey is better than sacrifice.” — 1 Samuel 15:22
Samuel’s message was not comfort.
It was judgment.
“Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD… the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines.” — 1 Samuel 28:18–19
Saul fell to the ground.
Not because he was holy.
Because he was exposed.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
This is the terrifying diagnosis:

Saul wanted guidance without surrender.
He wanted relief without repentance.
He wanted God’s voice while rejecting God’s authority.
And many people today are doing the same thing.

You want peace, but not obedience.
You want blessing, but not repentance.
You want Jesus as Savior, but not Lord.
God saw it.
But Saul’s story points us to the better King.

Saul failed.
Jesus obeyed.

Saul trembled before judgment.
Jesus bore judgment on the cross.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” — 1 Timothy 1:15
The answer is not spiritual curiosity.
The answer is repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.

Turn from sin.
Run to Christ.
Grace is still open.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 7 Roles as a Christian Employee
paragraphs: 7 Roles as a Christian Employee

You don’t clock in just to earn.
You clock in to represent.
Seven roles. One mission.

1. The Light in the System
You don’t blend in—you shine. Quiet integrity. Consistent excellence.
Even when no one is watching.
📖 “Let your light shine before others…” (Matthew 5:16)

2. The Servant, Not the Star
You’re not there to be applauded. You’re there to serve.
Emails. Deadlines. Small tasks. Holy ground.
📖 “Whoever wants to become great must be your servant.” (Mark 10:43)

3. The Integrity Carrier
You don’t bend truth to survive.
You stand—even if it costs you promotion.
Because character is louder than credentials.
📖 “The righteous walk in integrity…” (Proverbs 20:7)

4. The Peacemaker in Chaos
Office politics? Gossip? Tension?
You don’t fuel it. You calm it.
Your presence lowers the noise.
📖 “Blessed are the peacemakers…” (Matthew 5:9)

5. The Excellence Builder
You don’t work just for your boss.
You work as if Jesus Himself signed your paycheck.
No shortcuts. No half-effort.
📖 “Work heartily, as for the Lord…” (Colossians 3:23)

6. The Silent Witness
You don’t always preach.
But your life speaks—loud.
Kindness. Patience. Faithfulness.
People notice what you don’t say.
📖 “Live such good lives… that they may see your good deeds…” (1 Peter 2:12)

7. The Gospel Carrier
And when the moment opens—
You don’t stay silent.
Because someone at your workplace is drowning quietly.
And Jesus is the only rescue.
📖 “Always be ready to give an answer…” (1 Peter 3:15)
But here’s what we miss…
You can do all seven—and still miss the point.
Because being a “good employee” doesn’t save you.
Only Jesus does.

We don’t work for salvation.
We work from salvation.

You were once lost in sin.
Self-driven. Approval-hungry. Broken.

But Christ stepped in.
Lived the life you couldn’t.
Died the death you deserved.
Rose again—to give you new identity.
Now you don’t just have a job.
You have a calling.
Someone in your workplace needs this truth.

From deadlines to destiny—
Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t just turn a page.
paragraphs: He didn’t just turn a page.
He rewrote the whole relationship.
That’s what it means when we say Jesus established a New Testament.

Not a new book first…
but a new covenant.
A covenant is a binding promise between God and His people. The old one—the Old Testament—was built on law. Commands. Sacrifices. Repeated offerings for sin.
And still… people kept breaking it.

Again.
And again.

Because the law can expose sin—
but it cannot heal the heart.
Then Jesus steps in.
At the table, before the cross, He lifts the cup and says:
“This cup is the new covenant in My blood…”
That line is explosive.

Because now, the covenant is no longer written on stone—
it’s sealed in His blood.

Not the blood of goats.
Not temporary covering.
His blood.

Once.
For all.
But here’s what we miss…
The New Testament isn’t just “God lowered the standard.”
No.
He fulfilled it.

Jesus lived the perfect life we couldn’t live…
then took the punishment we deserved.
So now, forgiveness isn’t earned.
It’s received.

The old covenant said:
“Obey, and you will live.”

The new covenant says:
“Believe, and you are made alive.”

Not behavior modification—
heart transformation.

Not religion—
relationship.
And this is where grace walks in.
Under the New Testament, your past doesn’t get the final word.

Your shame?
Covered.

Your guilt?
Paid for.

Your identity?
Rewritten in Christ.
But don’t mistake grace for permission to stay the same.

Grace doesn’t excuse sin.
It breaks its power.

Because the same Jesus who forgives you—
also changes you.
From the inside out.
So what does it mean?
It means you don’t have to keep trying to earn what Jesus already finished.

It means you can come—right now—
with your mess, your failure, your hidden battles…
…and find mercy.
Come back to Him.

Not with promises.
But with surrender.

Say it simply:
“Jesus, I trust what You did for me.”

And watch how a new covenant
becomes a new life.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Unity in the body of Christ — Ephesians 4
paragraphs: Unity in the body of Christ — Ephesians 4
They didn’t break the church with a sword.
They broke it with ego.
One wanted the spotlight. Another wanted control. Someone got offended. Someone stopped listening. And suddenly the Body of Christ started fighting itself like it forgot whose Body it was.

That is why Ephesians 4 does not begin with platform.
It begins with posture.

“Walk worthy.”
With humility.
With gentleness.
With patience.
Bearing with one another in love.

That is not weakness.
That is spiritual maturity under pressure.

But here’s what we miss: unity is not pretending we are all the same. Unity is sinners saved by the same Christ, filled by the same Spirit, held together by the same grace. One body. One Spirit. One hope. One Lord. One faith. One baptism. One God and Father of all.

And that means division is never just a personality problem.
It is a Gospel problem.

Because Jesus did not bleed to build isolated believers with private opinions and public bitterness. He gave gifts to the church, called every member to grow, and commanded the Body to build itself up in love. Not in pride. Not in competition. In love.

So if there is envy in your heart, repent.
If there is offense you keep feeding, surrender it.
If there is a brother or sister you have reduced to an enemy, remember the cross.
Christ is not glorified when His Body tears itself apart.
He is glorified when broken people kneel low, forgive deeply, speak truth in love, and grow up into Him.

This is the call of Ephesians 4:
Stop acting like fragments.
Live like one Body.
Under one Head.
Jesus Christ.

And here’s the hope—unity does not start with us trying harder. It starts with Christ changing our hearts. The same Savior who forgives our sin can also kill our pride, heal our wounds, and teach us to love His people again.

Church, come back to the cross.
That is where division dies.
That is where unity begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Time Elisha Cursed Kids and Bears Attacked — 2 Kings 2:23–24
paragraphs: The Time Elisha Cursed Kids and Bears Attacked — 2 Kings 2:23–24
Not every Bible story feels easy to love.
This one feels dangerous.

Elisha walks up the road. A crowd comes out. They mock him: “Go up, baldhead.” Then he pronounces a curse in the name of the Lord… and two bears tear through them.
2 Kings 2:23–24.

And people ask:
“Why would God do that over an insult?”
But here’s what we miss.

This was not a cute scene with harmless toddlers teasing a prophet. The Hebrew can refer to youths or young men, and many scholars see this as a hostile mob, not playful children. And the phrase “Go up” may have been more than mockery of Elisha’s baldness—it may have been a sneering rejection of Elijah’s prophetic ascent, as if to say, “Why don’t you disappear too?” This was contempt for God’s messenger, in a place already soaked in rebellion.
Bethel.
A center of covenant compromise. A city with a history of false worship.

So this moment is not about fragile ego.
It is about defiant hearts mocking the Word of God.
That is why the story lands so hard. Because it exposes something in us. We want a God who comforts, but not a God who confronts. We want mercy without holiness. Grace without fear of the Lord.
But the same God who judged rebellion is the God who sent His Son to bear judgment for rebels like us.
That’s the Gospel.

Jesus took the curse so mockers could become worshipers.
Jesus bore wrath so sinners could receive mercy.
Jesus died and rose so hard hearts could be made new.

So yes—2 Kings 2 should sober us.
Do not laugh at holiness.
Do not despise the Word of the Lord.
Do not play with rebellion.
But do not stop at the bears.
Look to the cross.
Because the Judge has made a way for the guilty to come home.
Repent. Believe. And receive the mercy that Elisha’s mockers never sought—but Christ freely offers now.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Danger of Small Compromises
paragraphs: The Danger of Small Compromises
It never starts with open rebellion.
It starts with just this once.

One hidden click.
One private conversation.
One ignored conviction.
One excuse dressed up as weakness.
And you told yourself, “It’s not that serious.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Small compromises do not stay small.
“Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.” — James 1:15
Read that again.

Sin does not announce its final destination.
It whispers the first step.

God saw it.
You knew.
You felt the warning in your spirit, but you negotiated with it. You called it stress. You called it loneliness. You called it curiosity. But heaven called it what it was: compromise.
Samson did not lose his strength in one moment. He played with danger long before Delilah cut his hair.
David did not fall with Bathsheba suddenly. He stayed home when kings went to war.
Peter did not deny Jesus out of nowhere. He followed at a distance first.
Distance always comes before denial.
“Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards.” — Song of Solomon 2:15

Small foxes.
Small cracks.
Small lies.
Small permissions.

And slowly, your prayer life gets quieter.
Your conviction gets duller.
Your Bible stays closed longer.
Your worship becomes performance.
Your repentance becomes delay.
That is the danger.
Not that you fall overnight.
But that you drift and still think you are standing.
“Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” — 1 Corinthians 10:12
But there is grace.
Jesus did not die only for the scandal everyone saw. He died for the secret compromises nobody knew.
Bring it into the light.
Repent. Turn. Run back to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9

This is not the moment to hide.
This is the moment to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Jahaziel
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Jahaziel

He wasn’t the king.
He wasn’t the warrior.
He was the voice God chose when fear filled the room.
Jahaziel.

A name many people skim past in 2 Chronicles 20.
But when Judah was surrounded, when the nation was trembling, when Jehoshaphat and the people stood helpless before a massive enemy—the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jahaziel. Not the celebrity. Not the headline name. Jahaziel. And through him came a word that still shakes anxious hearts today:
“Do not be afraid or discouraged because of this vast army. For the battle is not yours, but God’s.” (2 Chronicles 20:15)

That line wasn’t spoken in comfort.
It was spoken in crisis.
And that’s what makes Jahaziel unforgettable.

He reminds us that God often hides thunder in overlooked people.
The room may ignore you.
The platform may never call your name.
But heaven knows exactly where to find a surrendered vessel.
But here’s what we miss—

Jahaziel’s moment was not really about Jahaziel.
It was about a God who steps into impossible situations and says, “Stand still. I will fight for you.” In the same way, the Gospel tells us the deepest battle was never ours to win. Sin was too strong. Death was too dark. We could not save ourselves. So Jesus stepped into our impossible war, carried our judgment on the cross, and rose in victory we could never produce on our own.

That is the greater word behind Jahaziel’s prophecy.
Not just, “God will handle your enemies.”
But, “In Christ, God has handled your greatest enemy already.”

So when fear starts preaching doom—remember Jahaziel.
When you feel unseen—remember Jahaziel.
When you think your only role is to stand in the crowd—remember Jahaziel.

God still uses surrendered voices.
God still speaks in dark hours.
God still wins battles His people cannot.

And maybe the character you almost overlooked…
was carrying the message your weary soul needed most.
Jesus is still saying: Do not fear. Stand firm. Watch what I will do.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He wasn’t killed.
paragraphs: He wasn’t killed.
He was betrayed by the boys who called him brother.

Joseph’s coat came back soaked in blood.
His father saw the garment.
And the lie did what lies do best.
It shattered a house.
Genesis 37.
But the real horror was not the torn robe.

It was the envy.
The hatred.
The slow-burning rage that smiled at Joseph one day and sold him the next.

His brothers did not just fake his death.
They buried truth under blood.
They weaponized grief.
They let their father mourn a son who was still breathing.
Sin does that.

It does not only wound the target.
It poisons everyone in the room.
But here’s what we miss…

Genesis 37 is not just about Joseph’s pain.
It is about the human heart without grace.
Jealousy can make family cruel.
Bitterness can make conscience go silent.
And unchecked sin will always demand another lie to keep the first one alive.
Yet even here, God was not absent.

Joseph was in a pit.
Then in chains.
Then in a foreign land.
But never outside the hand of God.

What his brothers meant for evil, God was already bending toward redemption.
Not because evil is good.
But because God is sovereign even over the schemes of broken men.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because Joseph points us to Someone greater.
Jesus was also betrayed.
Not for twenty pieces of silver only—but by the full weight of our sin.
He was stripped.
Rejected.
Handed over.
And unlike Joseph, He truly did die.

But on the third day, Christ rose again so liars, betrayers, the jealous, the bitter, the guilty—
people like us—
could be forgiven and made new.
This story is not only a warning.
It is an invitation.

Bring your hidden envy to Jesus.
Bring your family wounds to Jesus.
Bring the lie you have been protecting to Jesus.

Because the blood of a goat covered a deception.
But the blood of Christ destroys it.

Repent.
Come clean.
There is mercy here.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Simon the sorcerer tries to buy power — Acts 8
paragraphs: Simon the sorcerer tries to buy power — Acts 8

He wanted the fire of God
without the God of fire.

Simon saw hands laid on people.
He saw the Spirit move.
He saw power fall.
And he reached for his wallet.
That is the scandal of Acts 8.

Not just a sorcerer in Samaria.
A man exposed.
A heart that wanted influence more than surrender, wonder more than holiness, platform more than repentance.

He believed enough to stay close.
But not enough to die to himself.

So when Simon told the apostles, “Give me this power also,” Peter did not pat him on the back. He cut straight to the cancer: “May your silver perish with you… your heart is not right before God.” (Acts 8:20–21)
Strong words.

Because sacred things cannot be bought.
The Holy Spirit is not merchandise.
Anointing is not for sale.
The kingdom of God does not bow to ambition dressed in religious language.
And here’s what we miss—

Simon is not just a villain from the first century.
He is a mirror.

Every time we want the spotlight without the cross.
Every time we crave gifting without godliness.
Every time we ask for ministry influence while secretly feeding pride.
We are standing too close to Simon.
But grace walks in where pride gets exposed.

Peter did not only rebuke him. He told him to repent.
That means the door was still open.
Mercy was still calling.
Even for a man who tried to purchase what only heaven can give.
That is the Gospel.

You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot earn the Spirit.
You cannot manipulate grace.
But what you could never purchase, Jesus gives freely to the repentant sinner.

At the cross, God did not offer a transaction.
He offered a rescue.

So come empty-handed.
Come honest.
Come broken.
The blood of Jesus is enough for the proud heart, the greedy heart, the performative heart, the heart that wanted ministry for self instead of Christ.

Repent.
Believe.
Receive what money never could.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You don’t survive this long by luck.
paragraphs: You don’t survive this long by luck.
Israel should have been erased.
Empires rose against her. Kings plotted against her. Armies surrounded her. Hatred followed her through centuries like a shadow that refused to die.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
There is protection you cannot see.
“The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand.” Psalm 121:5
God saw it.

He saw Pharaoh.
He saw Haman.
He saw Rome.
He saw every nation that said, “Let us wipe them out.”
And still Israel remained.
Not because Israel was perfect.
Scripture is clear: sin brings judgment. Rebellion brings discipline. God does not overlook wickedness, not in Israel, not in the Church, not in you.
“You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Amos 3:2
Read that again.

Chosen does not mean untouched.
Chosen means accountable.
And that should shake you, because you thought God’s patience meant permission.
You knew.
You knew when you kept returning to the same sin. You knew when you prayed with your lips but wandered with your heart. You knew when conviction came and you silenced it.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Yet even in judgment, God’s covenant mercy speaks louder than the grave.
“He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” Psalm 121:4
The same God who preserved Israel is the God who sent Jesus Christ to save sinners.

Not by bloodline.
Not by religion.
Not by good behavior.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works.” Ephesians 2:8-9
Jesus is the true protection your soul needs.
Because the greatest enemy is not a nation outside your borders.
It is sin inside your heart.
And Christ did not come to decorate your life. He came to rescue it.
On the cross, judgment fell. Grace opened. Blood spoke. The Savior rose.
So repent.
Turn from sin. Trust Jesus. Stop hiding behind spiritual language while your heart stays cold.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Risk of Going Back to Old Habits — 2 Peter 2:22
paragraphs: The Risk of Going Back to Old Habits — 2 Peter 2:22

You washed the outside.
But the old appetite is still whispering.

“That dog returns to its vomit…”
Peter did not choose soft words. He chose a mirror.
“And a sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire” (2 Peter 2:22).
This is the danger of going back.

Not just making a mistake.
Not just stumbling in weakness.
But turning back to the very chains Jesus called you out of.

Old habits never come back wearing warning labels.
They come back dressed like comfort.
Like nostalgia.
Like relief.
Like “just this once.”
But sin never stays small. It always wants the throne.
And here’s what we miss…

Going back is not only about behavior.
It is about desire.
The hands follow what the heart secretly still worships.
That is why behavior management alone cannot save a soul.
You can wash a pig. You cannot change its nature.
Only Christ can do that.

Jesus did not die just to make you look clean.
He died and rose again to make you new.
New heart. New hunger. New direction.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Try harder not to go back.”
The Gospel is God saying, “Come to My Son and be transformed.”

So if you feel the pull of old habits today, do not flirt with them.
Expose them.
Confess them.
Kill them at the cross.
Run to the One who does not just clean the stain—but breaks the slavery.

You are not called to recycle your old life.
You are called to bury it with Christ.

There is hope.
Even for the one who feels the mud still calling.
Even for the one ashamed of how familiar the vomit looks.
Grace is still stronger.
Repentance is still open.
And Jesus still receives sinners who are ready to come home for real.

Don’t go back to what almost destroyed you.
The cross was too costly.
Your calling is too holy.
And Christ is too good.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He had ink on his skin…
paragraphs:
He had ink on his skin…
and shame in his soul.
He thought both were permanent.
So he asked the question people are often too afraid to say out loud:
“Did I disqualify myself from Heaven… because of this?”
Pause.
Let’s cut through the noise—religion can be loud, but Scripture is clear.

Some people point to Leviticus 19:28: “Do not mark your bodies…”
Yes, that verse exists.
But here’s what we miss…

That command was given to Israel in a specific cultural context—linked to pagan mourning rituals and idol worship.
It wasn’t about modern tattoos the way we understand them today.
And more importantly—
Heaven has never been earned by clean skin.
Not once.
Not ever.
Let me say it plain, kapatid:

Tattoos don’t send people to hell.
Sin does.

And sin is deeper than ink.
It’s in the heart.

Pride.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
No tattoo artist can etch that out.
But here’s where everything shifts.

Jesus didn’t come for perfect bodies.
He came for broken souls.

On the cross, He didn’t ask,
“Are you marked?”

He asked,
“Will you come?”

Because salvation is not about what’s on your skin—
it’s about who reigns in your heart.
“If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart… you will be saved.” (Romans 10:9)

No fine print.
No tattoo clause.
And here’s the scandal of grace:

A man with a past…
a body full of ink…
a life full of regret…
can kneel before Jesus—
and walk away cleaner than someone who never touched a needle.
Why?
Because the blood of Christ goes deeper than any ink ever could.
So can people with tattoos go to Heaven?
Yes—if they belong to Jesus.
And no—if they reject Him.
Same standard for everyone.
But let me ask you something more serious than tattoos:
Is your heart surrendered… or just your appearance?
Because God is not scanning your skin.
He’s reading your soul.

Come as you are.
Ink, scars, past, كلها.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He survived the king.
paragraphs: He survived the king.
He survived the crowd.
He survived the altar’s madness.
But one conversation under a tree destroyed him.

In 1 Kings 13, the man of God was sent with a clear word from the Lord: deliver the message, do not eat, do not drink, do not return the same way. And he obeyed—at first. He rebuked a wicked altar. He watched God split it open. He even saw judgment fall in real time.
Powerful.
Anointed.
Used by God.
And still… he died by a lion.
Why?
Not because God’s voice was unclear.
Because he let another voice override the one God had already spoken.
That is terrifying.

You can preach truth and still drift in private.
You can carry fire in public and compromise in secret.
You can be right at the altar and wrong under the shade tree.
And here’s what we miss: the old prophet’s lie only worked because it sounded spiritual. “An angel spoke to me…” That is how deception often enters—not looking rebellious, but looking religious.
This story is not just about a prophet.
It is about us.

Every time God has made His Word plain, but we keep shopping for a softer version.
Every time conviction was clear, but we waited for someone to tell us what our flesh wanted to hear.
Every time we traded obedience for comfort.
The lion in the story is a warning: delayed compromise still kills.
But thank God this is not where the Bible ends.

Because where the prophet failed, Jesus never did.
When the tempter came, Christ did not bend to a second voice.
He stood on the Word.
He obeyed perfectly.
And at the cross, He took the judgment our disobedience deserved.

So this is the hope: your failure does not have to be your funeral.
Repent.
Return.
Listen again to the voice of God in Scripture.
Jesus still restores people who wandered after the wrong voice.
Stop negotiating with what God already said.
Obedience is life. Christ is mercy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re not “standing your ground.”
paragraphs: You’re not “standing your ground.”
You might be resisting God.
And that’s more dangerous than you think.

Because sometimes the thing you’re protecting…
is the very thing God is asking you to lay down.
Here are 4 signs you’re defending what God wants you to surrender:

1. You keep justifying it instead of praying about it.
You’ve got reasons. Logic. Explanations.
But deep down—you haven’t brought it to God honestly.
Because you already know what He’ll say.
“And we know…” (Romans 8:28) — but we only quote that when it benefits us.

2. Correction feels like attack.
When someone speaks truth, you get defensive fast.
Walls go up. Tone changes.
Why? Because light is touching something you don’t want exposed.
“But whoever lives by the truth comes into the light…” (John 3:21)

3. You call it “peace” but it’s really avoidance.
You say, “I just want peace.”
But real peace doesn’t come from ignoring conviction.
It comes from surrender.
Jonah slept in the storm—
not because he had peace,
but because he was running.

4. Jesus isn’t Lord over that area.
Be honest.
You love Him… but not there.
Not that relationship.
Not that habit.
Not that secret.
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46)
But here’s what we miss…

God isn’t trying to take from you.
He’s trying to free you.

That thing you’re gripping so tightly?
It’s already costing you more than surrender ever will.
The cross proves it.

Jesus Christ didn’t defend His rights.
He surrendered them.

Not because He was weak—
but because love was stronger.

And through that surrender…
came your salvation.
So what are you still holding onto?

Pride?
Control?
A relationship God already warned you about?
A version of your life you refuse to release?
Let it go.

Not because it’s easy.
But because He’s worthy.

And because on the other side of surrender…
is freedom you’ve never tasted.

From hidden battles to holy freedom—
because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You were never meant to stay who your pain made you.
paragraphs: You were never meant to stay who your pain made you.
Romans 8:29 does not say God is trying to make you richer, more admired, or more comfortable.
It says He is making you like His Son.
That changes everything.

Some of us are frustrated because we keep asking, “Lord, when will my life finally look the way I imagined?”
But heaven is asking a deeper question: “Are you becoming who Christ died for you to be?”
Romans 8:29 says, “For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son…”

That means your breaking is not random.
Your pruning is not pointless.
Your waiting is not wasted.

God is not just managing your circumstances.
He is shaping your character.
He is cutting away what looks like you—but does not look like Jesus.
And that part hurts.

Because becoming who God called you to be will cost you the masks.
The counterfeit loves.
The old cravings.
The pride that made you feel strong while keeping you spiritually sick.
But here’s what we miss:

God’s goal is not to destroy your identity.
It is to redeem it.

Sin deformed us.
Grace reforms us.
Jesus restores what rebellion ruined.

You are not being called to invent a better version of yourself.
You are being called to surrender so Christ can be seen in you.
That is the Gospel.

The sin that stained you can be forgiven.
The shame that named you does not get the final word.
The patterns that chained you are not stronger than the Spirit of God.

In Christ, you are not trapped in who you were.
You are being transformed into who He already saw when He called you.

So do not run from the process.
Do not curse the fire that is burning off what cannot go where God is taking you.

Becoming hurts.
But becoming holy is worth it.

And when God is finished, your story will not shout your greatness.
It will reveal His Son.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When You Know the Truth but Resist It — John 3:19
paragraphs: When You Know the Truth but Resist It — John 3:19
You can know the truth… and still hate what it exposes.
That is the terror of John 3:19.
“And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.”
Jesus did not say the light failed to shine.
He said people saw it.
And resisted it.

That is what makes sin so dangerous. Not just that it blinds us. It makes us protective of our blindness. We defend what is killing us. We rename rebellion. We justify compromise. We hide behind image, religion, excuses, and polished words because deep down, we know the light is not merely informing us.
It is confronting us.
But here’s what we miss.
The Light came anyway.

Jesus did not enter the world to shame broken people from a distance. He stepped into our darkness to rescue us from it. He sees the secret. He knows the resistance. He knows the double life, the delayed obedience, the half-surrender, the truth you keep pushing away.
And still He calls.
Still He reaches.
Still He saves.
The tragedy is not that truth is unavailable.
The tragedy is that pride makes us flinch when grace is standing at the door.

Beloved, if the Word of God is exposing something in you right now, do not run from the Light. Run into it. Conviction is not cruelty. It is mercy. The Lord only uncovers what He intends to heal through Christ.
You do not have to keep defending the dark.
Jesus is better.

Bring the secret into the Savior’s presence. Confess it. Repent of it. Surrender it. There is no sin so deeply buried that the blood of Christ cannot cleanse it. There is no darkness so stubborn that the risen Jesus cannot overcome it.

This is the hope:
the same Light that exposes you
is the Light that can free you.

Come into the Light.
And live.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He waited decades for the promise.
paragraphs:
He waited decades for the promise.
Then God asked him to put it on the altar.

That’s not a small test.
That’s everything.

In Genesis 22, God tells Abraham:
“Take your son… your only son Isaac, whom you love… and offer him.”
Pause there.

God wasn’t confused.
He wasn’t cruel.
He was exposing something deeper than obedience—
the throne of Abraham’s heart.

Isaac wasn’t just a son.
He was the promise.
The future.
The proof that God keeps His word.
And that’s exactly why God touched it.

Because sometimes the greatest gift God gives you
can quietly take the place of God Himself.
But here’s what we miss…
God never intended Isaac to die.

The command was a test (Genesis 22:1), not a trap.
A revelation, not a destruction.

Abraham walks up that mountain carrying fire and a knife—
but also carrying faith.

Hebrews 11 says he believed
God could raise Isaac from the dead.

That means this wasn’t blind obedience.
This was fierce trust.

“Even if I don’t understand…
I know who God is.”
And at the final moment—
God stops the knife.
A ram appears.
A substitute is given.
Sound familiar?

Because that mountain whispers forward
to another Father…
another Son…
At the cross, God did not stop the sacrifice.
Jesus became the Lamb.

Where Isaac was spared,
Christ was not.
So you could be.
Why did God ask for Isaac?

Not because He wanted blood—
but because He wanted Abraham’s full trust.

Not because He delights in pain—
but because He reveals where we place our hope.
And in the end, Abraham didn’t lose his son.

He gained a deeper revelation:
“The Lord will provide.” (Yahweh Yireh)

If God touches something in your life—
a relationship, a dream, a future—
it’s not always removal.
Sometimes it’s invitation.
“Will you trust Me… even here?”
What’s your “Isaac”?
Lay it down.

Because anything surrendered to God
is never truly lost—
it’s placed in the hands of the One
who gave His Son for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They didn’t break the Church from the outside.
paragraphs: They didn’t break the Church from the outside.
We helped from within.
Quietly. Respectably. In Sunday clothes.
Here are 7 ways we partner with darkness without even realizing it—

1. We tolerate “small” sin.
Not the scandalous kind. The “manageable” kind. Pride. Gossip. Lust in secret.
We call it weakness. God calls it poison.
“Be holy…” (1 Peter 1:16)

2. We replace repentance with routine.
We show up. Sing loud. Lift hands.
But never surrender.
Church attendance without heart transformation is spiritual theater.

3. We divide over preferences, not truth.
Music style. Leadership style. Personal offense.
The enemy doesn’t need to destroy us—just divide us.
“But if you bite and devour one another…” (Galatians 5:15)

4. We elevate leaders above Christ.
When a pastor falls, our faith collapses.
Why? Because we built on personality, not the Person of Jesus.
Only Christ is unshakable.

5. We stay silent when truth costs us.
We fear losing approval more than losing purity.
So we whisper truth in private… and compromise in public.
That silence? It’s not neutral. It’s surrender.

6. We play with temptation instead of fleeing it.
We scroll longer. Chat deeper. Linger closer.
Then act surprised when we fall.
“Flee youthful lusts…” (2 Timothy 2:22)

7. We forget the Gospel is for us too.
We preach grace to others—but live condemned ourselves.
Or worse—we stop preaching grace at all.
A Church without the Gospel becomes a museum of masks.
But here’s what we miss…
Jesus already saw all this—and still chose the Church.

Not because we’re clean.
But because He makes us clean.

The cross is not just where sinners are forgiven—
It’s where the Church is rebuilt.
Right now.
Right here.

Repentance is not humiliation.
It’s restoration.

Grace is not permission.
It’s power.

So if this pierced something in you—good.
That’s not shame. That’s the Spirit calling you home.
Come back.

Not to religion.
To Jesus.

He doesn’t abandon His Church.
He purifies it.
And He’s not done with you.
Pray through it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Esau weeps for lost blessing — Genesis 27
paragraphs: Esau weeps for lost blessing — Genesis 27
He wasn’t crying because he lost a meal.
He was crying because he lost a blessing he treated like it was cheap.

Esau wept in Genesis 27 not because Jacob was stronger, but because a moment of appetite had already sold what his tears could not recover. He despised his birthright in Genesis 25, and by Genesis 27, the consequences had a voice. Bitter. Loud. Irreversible in that moment.
That is the terror of sin.

You can laugh with it early.
You can justify it quickly.
You can call it small.
But one day it shows up with a receipt.

Esau said, “Bless me—me also, O my father!” and then lifted up his voice and wept. The pain is real. The regret is real. But here’s what we miss: tears alone do not save. Sorrow alone does not restore. You can cry and still not repent. You can grieve consequences and still not surrender your heart to God.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because where Esau lost a blessing he could not reclaim, sinners like us are offered something better in Christ that we do not deserve. Jesus took the place of the undeserving. Jesus carried the curse. Jesus opens the door for rebels, failures, schemers, and broken men who realize too late that they traded eternity for appetite. In Christ, repentance is still open. Mercy is still calling. The cross says your worst exchange does not have to be the end of your story.

Do not wait until sin becomes loss.
Do not wait until hunger becomes heartbreak.
Do not trade holy things for temporary cravings.
Run to Jesus now.
Because in Him, what shame tried to bury, grace can still resurrect.

Hebrews 12:16–17 warns us not to be like Esau—godless, impulsive, driven by appetite, grieving the loss but not turning to God. That warning is not there to crush you. It is there to wake you up. Christ is still receiving the repentant.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was doing nothing.
paragraphs: She was doing nothing.
At least that’s how it looked.

Martha was moving. Serving. Sweating. Carrying the weight of the room.
Mary was sitting.
And Jesus defended the one who looked less productive.

“Mary… sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to His teaching.”
— Luke 10:39
That verse cut me deep.
Because I’ve been Martha more times than I want to admit.

Busy for God.
Working for God.
Serving around Jesus…
but not slowing down to be with Jesus.

And that is the lesson that humbled me:
Activity is not always intimacy.
You can fill the house with service and still leave your soul empty.
You can prepare meals, organize ministry, help everyone else—
and still miss the voice of the One you claim to love.
But here’s what we miss…

Jesus never rebuked Martha for serving.
He rebuked her for being worried and distracted.

That means the real danger is not work.
It is work that pulls your heart away from worship.
It is service without stillness.
Ministry without presence.
Hands full.
Heart far.

Mary chose the better portion not because she was lazy—
but because she understood something eternal:
Before we do anything for Christ, we must first learn to sit at His feet.

That’s where strength is born.
That’s where peace returns.
That’s where your soul stops performing and starts receiving.

Some of us are exhausted not because we are doing too much,
but because we are doing much without drinking deeply from Jesus.

Sit first.
Listen first.
Love Him first.
Then serve from fullness, not frenzy.

And here’s the Gospel:
Jesus is not looking for frantic performance.
He is calling for surrendered presence.
He didn’t die and rise again just to make you useful.
He saved you so you could know Him, walk with Him, and be transformed by Him.

So today, don’t just ask,
“What do I need to do?”
Ask,
“Have I been with Him?”

Because the better portion is still available.
And His name is Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Saul fears people more than God — 1 Samuel 15
paragraphs: Saul fears people more than God — 1 Samuel 15
He didn’t lose the kingdom in battle.
He lost it because he was more afraid of people than of God.
Saul’s confession in 1 Samuel 15 is chilling: “I have sinned… I feared the people and obeyed their voice.” Saul looked like a king on the outside, but inside, he was being ruled by the crowd.
That’s the danger.

A man can wear a crown and still be a slave.
A woman can look strong and still be controlled by applause.
You can sit in church, serve faithfully, smile publicly—
and still let the opinions of people become louder than the voice of God.
Saul spared what God told him to destroy. Not because God was unclear. Because obedience got expensive.
And that’s where many fall.

We fear rejection.
We fear being misunderstood.
We fear losing people, status, comfort, image.
So we adjust. We soften conviction. We rename compromise. We keep what God said surrender.
But here’s what we miss: the fear of man will always make you disobey God, and disobedience always costs more than you planned to pay.
Saul wanted public honor more than holy surrender. That is why his crown slipped before his life was over.
But the story doesn’t end there for us.

Because where Saul failed, Jesus obeyed perfectly. Christ did not bow to the crowd. He did not surrender to public pressure. He set His face toward the cross and obeyed the Father completely. And through His blood, fearful people like us can be forgiven, changed, and made bold again.

So repent where Saul refused.
Tear down the idol of human approval.
Ask God for a heart that trembles at His Word more than at human opinion.

Better to lose applause and keep obedience
than gain approval and grieve God.

Fear God.
Love people.
But never reverse those two.
“The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is safe.” — Proverbs 29:25
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Churches in Revelation Were Warnings for Today
paragraphs: The Churches in Revelation Were Warnings for Today
You thought Revelation was only about the end of the world.
But before God revealed beasts, judgments, trumpets, and fire…
He spoke to the Church.
Not the world.
The Church.
Read that again.
Jesus walked among the lampstands and exposed what looked alive but was dying.
Ephesus had truth but lost love.
Smyrna suffered but stayed faithful.
Pergamum compromised.
Thyatira tolerated sin.

Sardis had a reputation for life, but Jesus said, “You are dead.”
Revelation 3:1
Philadelphia was weak, but faithful.
Laodicea was rich, comfortable, and spiritually disgusting.
Jesus said:

“Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.”
Revelation 3:16
God saw it.
You knew.

The private compromise.
The worship with no surrender.
The sermons without repentance.
The church attendance without obedience.
The Bible posts without brokenness.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus didn’t warn them because He hated them.
He warned them because He loved them.

“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent.”
Revelation 3:19
That is the mercy of Christ.

He exposes before He removes.
He convicts before He judges.
He knocks before the door closes.

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.”
Revelation 3:20
This is not a game.
A church can have lights, music, branding, programs, and crowds…
and still have Jesus outside the door.
The warning is not just for ancient churches.
It is for today.

For pastors.
For believers.
For the lukewarm.
For the religious.
For the ones who still know how to look saved while hiding sin.
Repent.

Not perform.
Not explain.
Not pretend.
Repent and return to Jesus Christ.
Because salvation is not found in church culture.
It is found in the crucified and risen King.

“In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses.”
Ephesians 1:7
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Search your heart. Open Revelation 2–3. Let Christ examine what everyone else applauds.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Jesus Did After Rising — Acts 1:3
paragraphs: What Jesus Did After Rising — Acts 1:3

He didn’t rise just to prove a point.
He stayed… to prepare a people.

Forty days.
That’s what Acts of the Apostles 1:3 tells us.

Forty days of a resurrected Jesus walking, teaching, revealing—
not to crowds chasing miracles,
but to disciples still wrestling with doubt.
He could have ascended that same morning.
But He didn’t.
Why?

Because resurrection wasn’t the finish line.
It was the beginning of a mission.

He showed them His scars.
Not hidden. Not erased.
Glorified wounds—proof that pain redeemed becomes power released.

He spoke about the Kingdom of God.
Not politics. Not revenge. Not overthrow.
Kingdom.
But here’s what we miss…
They still didn’t get it.

They asked, “Lord, will You restore the kingdom to Israel now?” (Acts 1:6)
They wanted crowns.
Jesus offered calling.
They expected takeover.
Jesus promised power—but not the kind they imagined.
“Wait,” He said.

Wait for the Spirit.
Wait for heaven’s fire.
Wait until weak men become witnesses.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because even after the resurrection—
they were still confused, still flawed, still slow.
And Jesus stayed anyway.

He didn’t cancel them.
He completed them.

He doesn’t rush broken people into purpose.
He walks with them until truth burns clear.
That same Jesus is still patient with you.

Still revealing.
Still restoring.
Still calling.

Your confusion doesn’t disqualify you.
Your delay doesn’t disinterest Him.
If you’re still here—He’s still working.

Forty days of proof.
A lifetime of purpose.

And then He ascended…
not to abandon—
but to send.
Because the story was never about staying with Him physically.

It was about Him living in us—through the Spirit—
turning ordinary people into living evidence of resurrection power.
So don’t rush your process.

Let Him teach you.
Let Him show you His scars.
Let Him reframe your expectations.

And when the Spirit comes—
you won’t just believe.
You’ll burn.

From confusion to commission—
because Jesus doesn’t just rise…
He raises people with Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… the temple was built in silence without hammer sounds?
paragraphs: Did you know… the temple was built in silence without hammer sounds?

No hammers.
No chisels.
No noise.
Just… obedience.

That detail isn’t random—it’s written in Scripture:
“The temple was built with stone prepared at the quarry, so that no hammer or chisel or any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.” (1 Kings 6:7)
Silence.
But don’t miss this.
The shaping still happened.
Just not in public.

We love loud transformations.
Big testimonies.
Visible breakthroughs.
Applause.
But God?
He often does His deepest work off-site.

Hidden.
Unseen.
Quiet.

The cutting.
The breaking.
The refining.
Not in the spotlight—but in the quarry.
And here’s the tension:

You want God to use you loudly…
But you resist being shaped quietly.

You want the platform…
But not the preparation.
But here’s what we miss:
The temple looked peaceful because the stones already endured the noise somewhere else.

The silence wasn’t absence of work.
It was evidence of completed surrender.

Some scholars interpret this as a picture of reverence—God’s house set apart from the chaos of construction.
But it also whispers something deeper:
God prepares His people before placing them.

So if your life feels like a quarry right now—
Pressure.
Cutting.
Isolation.
Don’t despise it.
That’s where God is fitting you.

Precisely.
Intentionally.
Lovingly.
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because you’re not just a stone.
You’re being built into something eternal.
“You also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house…” (1 Peter 2:5)
And the cornerstone?
Jesus Christ.

He was rejected.
Broken.
Crucified.
Not in silence—but in suffering.
So you could be placed in glory.
You don’t earn your place in God’s house.
You receive it through Christ.

Through repentance.
Through surrender.
Through grace.
So stay in the process.

Even when it’s quiet.
Especially when it’s quiet.
God is building something holy out of your hidden season.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 🚨 YOU THINK YOU’RE LOSING… BUT WHAT IF YOU’RE BEING SET FREE?
paragraphs: 🚨 YOU THINK YOU’RE LOSING… BUT WHAT IF YOU’RE BEING SET FREE?
You keep holding on…

To that relationship.
To that plan.
To that version of your life you don’t want to let go of.
Because deep down, you believe:
👉 “If I surrender this… I lose.”
But that belief?
It’s the very thing keeping you stuck.
“Surrender Feels Like Loss—Until You Understand It”
This is not a soft devotional.
This is a confrontation.

A wake-up call for believers who say they trust God…
but still cling to control when it matters most.
Because the truth is:

You’re not afraid of losing it…
You’re afraid God’s way might cost you more than you want to pay.
🔥 WHAT THIS BOOK WILL DO IN YOU:

• Expose why surrender feels painful (and why that’s actually a sign God is working)
• Reveal what God is REALLY removing from your life
• Break the illusion that control equals safety
• Show you how to trust God when nothing makes sense
• Help you step into real freedom—not fake comfort

If you’ve been stuck in cycles…
delayed obedience…
or quiet resistance to God…
This will hit you.
⚖️ REAL TALK:

Most people say “I trust God”…
but panic when He asks them to let go.

Most want freedom…
but refuse surrender.

Most pray for change…
but protect the very thing God is trying to remove.
But a few?

A few choose obedience—even when it hurts.
A few surrender—and actually transform.
👉 Which one are you?
🔐 THIS IS NOT FOR EVERYONE

A growing movement of believers who are done playing church
and ready to walk in real transformation.
Inside you’ll get:

• Daily faith-building content
• Spiritual discipline systems
• Real teaching—not surface-level motivation

If you’re tired of pretending…
If you’re done holding onto what God told you to release…
If you’re ready to actually grow—
Step into the life you keep praying for.
💬 ENGAGE
This isn’t just a book.
It’s a turning point.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You thought fasting was just about food.
paragraphs: You thought fasting was just about food.
But heaven saw the hunger underneath.
Daniel said, “I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth…” and for twenty-one days, nothing seemed to move.

No breakthrough.
No answer.
No sign.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The delay was not denial.
The angel said, “From the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand… thy words were heard.”
From the first day.

God heard you before you felt anything.
God moved before you saw anything.
God answered before the battle became visible.
God saw it.

He saw the plate you pushed away.
He saw the secret prayer you whispered with tears in your throat.
He saw the phone you wanted to pick up, the sin you almost ran back to, the comfort you almost chose over consecration.
You knew.

You knew this fast was not about looking spiritual.
It was war.
Because some chains do not break while you keep feeding the flesh.
Jesus said, “This kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.”

Not performance.
Not religion.
Not proving yourself.
Surrender.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
Daniel fasted, but heaven responded because his heart was set before God.
And that is where many miss it.

You can skip meals and still feed pride.
You can avoid food and still feast on lust.
You can drink water and still swallow bitterness.
The fast God responds to is not empty hands with a full ego.
It is repentance.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
Read that again.
A clean heart.
Jesus Christ did not die so you could manage sin better. He died to redeem you from it. The cross is where your rebellion was exposed, your debt was paid, and grace became greater than your guilt.
So do not just ask God for an answer.
Ask Him for a new heart.
Because when earth bows, heaven responds.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Are You Growing or Stuck? — 2 Peter 3:18
paragraphs: Are You Growing or Stuck? — 2 Peter 3:18

Some people call it “rest.”
But deep down, it’s drift.

Some call it “waiting on God.”
But really, they stopped pursuing Him.
Are you growing… or just getting older in church?
“But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be glory both now and forever! Amen.” — 2 Peter 3:18

Peter did not say stay inspired.
He said grow.

That means grace is not a hiding place for spiritual laziness.
Grace is the power that pulls you closer to Jesus.

You can attend services.
Post verses.
Say “God knows my heart.”
And still be stuck in the same pride, the same compromise, the same coldness.
But here’s what we miss…

Growth is not perfection.
Growth is repentance.
Growth is hunger.
Growth is letting Christ confront what you keep excusing.

A growing believer is not sinless.
But they are not settled in sin.
They do not play with darkness and call it maturity.
They keep coming back to the feet of Jesus.

Because the Gospel does not just forgive your past.
It transforms your present.

Jesus did not die and rise again so you could remain spiritually numb.
He came to save you fully.
To break what has been binding you.
To form His life in you.
To teach your heart to love holiness again.
So ask yourself with trembling honesty:

Am I growing in grace?
Am I growing in the knowledge of Christ?
Do I know Him more deeply now than I did before?
Or have I learned how to look alive while staying stuck?

Beloved, there is no shame in admitting you’ve been stagnant.
The danger is pretending you’re fine.

Today, Christ still calls dry hearts back.
Today, mercy still opens the door.
Today, the Holy Spirit still grows those who surrender.

You are not doomed to stay where you are.
In Jesus, stuck is not your final state.

Repent.
Return.
Grow again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Happens After the Resurrection Season — Acts 1:3
paragraphs: What Happens After the Resurrection Season — Acts 1:3
He didn’t just rise… He stayed.
For forty days.

Not to prove a point—
but to prepare a people.
“After his suffering, he presented himself to them and gave many convincing proofs that he was alive. He appeared to them over a period of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God.” — Acts 1:3
Let that sit.

Jesus didn’t rush back to heaven.
He walked with them. Ate with them. Taught them. Rebuilt what fear had shattered.

Because resurrection isn’t the end of the story—
it’s the beginning of your assignment.
You’d think the miracle was enough.

The empty tomb.
The pierced hands now breathing.
Death undone.
But here’s what we miss…
They still didn’t get it.

They saw Him—yet still asked,
“Lord, are you at this time going to restore the kingdom to Israel?”

They wanted power.
Jesus offered purpose.

They expected a throne.
Jesus promised a Spirit.
And that’s where grace walks in.

He didn’t rebuke their slowness.
He discipled it.

For forty days, He shifted their vision—
from earthly crowns to eternal commission.

From “What do we get?”
to “Who will we reach?”

Resurrection season is not about comfort.
It’s about calling.

Jesus stays close not just to comfort your pain—
but to confront your direction.

He will sit with you…
until your heart burns again.

He will speak…
until confusion becomes commission.

He will remain…
until you’re ready to be sent.
And then?
He ascends.

Not to abandon—
but to empower.

Because Acts doesn’t start with a miracle.
It starts with men who were finally ready.

So if you’re in a “forty-day season” right now—
waiting, unsure, in-between…
Don’t rush it.

God is not delaying you.
He is forming you.

Jesus is alive.
Not just to amaze you—
but to assign you.

And the same Spirit He promised them…
He offers you.
Repent. Believe. Follow.

The story didn’t end at the resurrection—
that’s where yours begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most People Miss This About God’s Timing With Abraham
paragraphs: Most People Miss This About God’s Timing With Abraham
He waited 25 years.

Not 25 minutes.
Not 25 months.
Twenty-five years for a promise God spoke in one moment.

We read Genesis like it’s a fast story.
But Abraham lived it in slow pain.

God said: “I will make you a father of many nations.” (Genesis 12:2)
But year after year… nothing happened.

No child.
No proof.
Just silence.
And here’s what most people miss:

God didn’t delay the promise.
He developed the man.

Because the version of Abraham who heard the promise…
was not yet the man who could carry it.
So God waited.

Not because He forgot.
Not because He changed His mind.
But because timing in heaven is not about calendars—
It’s about character.
But here’s what we miss…

In the waiting, Abraham stumbled.
He tried to “help” God through Hagar (Genesis 16).
He got tired of trusting.
Sound familiar?

We rush.
We force.
We settle.
Because delay feels like denial.
But it’s not.
Delay is often God’s mercy.

Because if God gave you everything you prayed for right now—
without shaping your heart—
it might destroy you instead of bless you.
And that’s where grace walks in.

When Isaac was finally born (Genesis 21),
it wasn’t just a baby.
It was proof.

That God keeps His Word.
That waiting is not wasted.
That even after failure—God’s promise still stands.
And listen carefully—

The same God who fulfilled His promise to Abraham
fulfilled the greatest promise through Jesus Christ.

Not late.
Not early.
Right on time.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
That’s the Gospel.

You don’t earn it.
You don’t rush it.
You receive it.

So if you’re in a season where nothing makes sense—
where prayers feel unanswered—
Don’t walk away.

God is not ignoring you.
He is preparing you.

Wait on Him.
Trust Him.
Run back to Jesus, not away from Him.
Because when God moves—
It will be undeniable.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You think fasting always changes the outcome… it doesn’t.
paragraphs: You think fasting always changes the outcome… it doesn’t.
The Stories They Never Tell

The King Who Fasted but Still Lost Everything
2 Samuel 12:16–18
He Fasted. Still Lost.

David lay on the ground, begging for the child’s life.
But heaven did not reverse the consequence.

The king refused food.
He wept through the night.
He pleaded with God in brokenness.
And still—the child died.
SCRIPTURE

“David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.” — 2 Samuel 12:16
“On the seventh day the child died.” — 2 Samuel 12:18
THE TENSION

David was not cold.
He was not casual.
He was desperate.

This was not fake religion.
This was a shattered father on the floor.
And still he lost what he was begging to keep.
BUT HERE’S WHAT WE MISS…

Fasting is not a tool to control God.
Tears are not leverage.
Brokenness is real—but real sorrow does not erase every earthly consequence.
That is the part they don’t preach.

David was forgiven.
But the sword still entered his house.
Grace covered his sin, but consequence still tore through his world.
GOSPEL CLARITY

This story is not telling you that prayer is useless.
It is telling you that God is still God.

You can repent and still grieve.
You can be forgiven and still feel the weight of what sin damaged.
You can be loved by God and still walk through painful consequences.

That is why we need more than tears.
We need a Savior.

Jesus did what David never could.
He did not lie on the ground begging for mercy for His own sin.
He went to the cross to secure mercy for ours.

David’s floor was sorrow.
Christ’s cross became salvation.
TRUTH BOMB

Repentance restores fellowship with God—but it does not always cancel the harvest of sin.
And yet even there, mercy still speaks.
CTA
Where sin tried to finish the story… Jesus wrote redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He swore he would never fall.
paragraphs: He swore he would never fall.

Not him.
Not Peter.
“Lord, I am ready to go with You both to prison and to death!” (see Gospel of Luke 22:33)

Bold words.
Loud loyalty.
Unbreakable—so he thought.

But a few hours later…
A servant girl asked a simple question.
And Peter broke.
Why did Peter deny Jesus Christ after promising everything?
Because zeal is not the same as surrender.

Peter loved Jesus—no doubt.
But his confidence was still in himself.

His courage was real…
Until pressure exposed its limits.
Luke 22:61–62 hits like thunder:
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter…”
That look.

Not anger.
Not rejection.
A look that pierced deeper than any accusation.
And Peter remembered.

Then he went out…
and wept bitterly.
But here’s what we miss…
Peter didn’t fall because he didn’t love Jesus.

He fell because he overestimated his strength
and underestimated his weakness.

He followed at a distance (Luke 22:54).
He warmed himself by the enemy’s fire.
He stayed close enough to watch—
but not close enough to stand.
That’s where denial begins.

Not in a moment—
but in a slow drift.
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because Peter’s story didn’t end in failure.

After the cross…
after the resurrection…
Jesus didn’t replace him.
He restored him.
“Do you love Me?” (John 21)

Three times denied.
Three times restored.
Not erased—redeemed.
Listen carefully:
Your worst moment is not your final chapter.

Yes, you may have said, “I’ll never do that”—
and still did.
Yes, fear may have silenced your faith.
Yes, you may be carrying the weight of a bitter failure.

But the same eyes that met Peter in his denial
are still looking at you—

Not to condemn…
but to call you back.
Come closer.

Not at a distance.
Not hiding by чужд fire.
Come near to Christ.

Because only in Him
does weak love become steadfast.

Only in Him
does failure become testimony.

Only in Him
does denial become redemption.
Come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They complained about food. God answered with fire in the flesh.
paragraphs: They complained about food. God answered with fire in the flesh.

Not because He was cruel.
Because their rebellion was no longer small.
Numbers 21:5–6 is terrifying for a reason.

Israel did not just grumble about the wilderness.
They spoke against God.
They despised the bread He provided.
They treated mercy like trash.
That is the real poison.

Not the snakes first.
The pride.

They said, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die?”
As if bondage was better than obedience.
As if slavery was sweeter than trusting God.
As if heaven’s provision was beneath them.
And then the serpents came.

Suddenly the people felt in their bodies what sin had already done in their hearts.
What was inside them became visible around them.
Complaint. Unbelief. Contempt.
Bitten by the very death they kept flirting with.
But here’s what we miss—

This story is not only about snakes.
It is about sin.
And sin still bites.

The tongue that keeps murmuring.
The heart that keeps accusing God.
The soul that keeps saying, “What You’ve given me is not enough.”
That road always ends in venom.
And yet grace walks into the scene.

Because later in this chapter, God tells Moses to lift up the bronze serpent.
Whoever looked in faith would live.
And Jesus takes that shocking image and says it pointed to Himself.

Lifted up.
So the poisoned could live.

This is the Gospel:
We were not dying because life was unfair.
We were dying because sin had already entered the bloodstream.
But Christ was lifted up on the cross so that everyone who looks to Him in faith will not perish, but have eternal life.

So do not just fear the snakes.
Fear the hard heart that complains against a holy God.
And do not stay there.

Repent.
Look to Jesus.
Live.

The same God who judged sin made a way for sinners to be healed.
That is not contradiction.
That is holy mercy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: War didn’t start in heaven.
paragraphs:
War didn’t start in heaven.
It started in the human heart.

Before bullets, there was pride.
Before bombs, there was envy.
Before nations rise against nations, a soul whispers, “I want what isn’t mine.”

And that’s where the question cuts deep:
Why doesn’t God stop wars?

He could.
One word—and every weapon would rust.
One breath—and every army would fall still.
But here’s what we miss…

God doesn’t just want to stop wars around us.
He came to end the war within us.

Because if He forced peace externally
while leaving the human heart untouched—
war would just be reborn tomorrow…
in a different field, under a different flag.

Jesus said it plainly:
“Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder…” (Matthew 15:19)
That’s the battlefield.

And God’s answer wasn’t silence.
It was a cross.

He didn’t stay distant from our violence.
He stepped into it.

Betrayed.
Beaten.
Crucified.

Not because He couldn’t stop it—
but because He chose to absorb it.

On that cross, Jesus took the full weight of human sin—
every hatred, every war, every drop of innocent blood—
and carried it into death.
And then…
He rose.

That’s not just hope for heaven someday.
That’s the only power strong enough to transform a human heart today.

Because peace on earth doesn’t begin with treaties.
It begins with surrender.

You can silence guns for a season.
Only Christ can silence the rage inside a soul.
So why doesn’t God stop wars immediately?

He’s doing something deeper.
Slower.
Eternal.

He’s rescuing hearts—one by one—
through Jesus.

And one day, He will end all wars completely.
Scripture promises a King who will “make wars cease to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 46:9).
But until that day, the invitation stands:

Lay down your weapons.
Your pride.
Your unforgiveness.
Let the Prince of Peace rule you first.

Because when Christ conquers a heart,
war loses ground.

From chaos to Christ—
because Jesus doesn’t just end wars…
He rewrites hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 5 Lessons God Teaches in Delay
paragraphs: 5 Lessons God Teaches in Delay

Delay isn’t denial.
But it feels like rejection, doesn’t it?

You prayed.
You fasted.
You believed.
And still… nothing.
Silence.
But here’s what we miss—God is never passive in your waiting. He is precise. Intentional. Fatherly.
Here are 5 lessons God teaches in delay:

1. Delay exposes what you really trust.
When the answer tarries, idols surface.
Control. People. Outcomes.
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart…” — Proverbs 3:5
Delay asks: Do you trust His hand… or just His gifts?

2. Delay purifies your motives.
At first, you want the blessing.
But in the waiting, God reshapes your desire until you want Him more.
“Delight yourself in the Lord…” — Psalm 37:4

Not just the promise.
The Promiser.

3. Delay builds strength you can’t rush.
Quick answers don’t build deep roots.
“Those who wait on the Lord shall renew their strength…” — Isaiah 40:31

Waiting is not weakness.
It’s training.

4. Delay aligns timing with purpose.
You see the now.
God sees the whole story.
“For the vision is yet for an appointed time…” — Habakkuk 2:3

Some doors must stay closed—
until you’re ready to walk through them without destroying what’s inside.

5. Delay deepens your dependence on grace.
And this is where everything shifts.

Because the greatest “delay” in history…
was actually salvation on schedule.

Jesus didn’t come early.
He came exactly when we needed Him.
“At just the right time, Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6
And on that cross, it looked like God was late.

But three days later—
we realized He was right on time.
So if you’re in delay right now… hear this:

God is not ignoring you.
He is preparing you.

And more than that—
He’s drawing you back to the only answer that truly satisfies:
Jesus Christ.

Not just the One who gives blessings—
but the One who is the blessing.
Because this isn’t wasted time.
This is holy ground.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 4 Signs You’re Speaking From Hurt
paragraphs: 4 Signs You’re Speaking From Hurt
4 signs you’re speaking from hurt.

Not wisdom.
Not boldness.
Hurt.
And wounded words can sound righteous while quietly bleeding on everyone around you.

1. You always need the last word.
Not because truth matters.
Because pain wants control.
A bruised heart doesn’t just speak. It swings.
But “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

2. You turn every disagreement into a personal attack.
Small correction. Big reaction.
Why? Because unresolved wounds make everything feel like rejection.
When the soul is raw, even gentle words can feel like knives.
“A gentle answer turns away wrath” (Proverbs 15:1).

3. Your words expose more bitterness than love.
Sarcasm. Shade. Cold truth without compassion.
You may be saying facts, but you’re no longer sounding like Jesus.
Because hurt loves to preach what it has not healed from.
And Scripture says, “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34).

4. You speak to punish, not to restore.
That’s the dangerous one.
When pain becomes your pulpit, people stop hearing grace.
You don’t just want to be understood.
You want someone else to feel what you felt.
But here’s what we miss:

Jesus never asked us to fake healing.
He asked us to bring Him the wound.

Because unhealed pain will preach.
It will parent.
It will lead.
It will love.
And it will keep spilling into every conversation until grace touches the root.

The Gospel is not behavior management.
It is heart resurrection.

Christ doesn’t shame you for speaking from hurt.
He invites you to be healed from it.
Repent. Slow down. Let the Holy Spirit search your heart. Let Jesus cleanse what pain has poisoned.

You do not have to keep speaking from the place that broke you.
In Christ, you can speak from peace.
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up…” (Ephesians 4:29)
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Why Secret Sin Feels Safe Until It Destroys You” — Luke 8:17
paragraphs: “Why Secret Sin Feels Safe Until It Destroys You” — Luke 8:17
You think nobody knows.
That is exactly why secret sin feels safe.

It hides in the dark.
It whispers, You’re still in control.
It lets you smile in public while your soul quietly rots in private.
And for a while, it works.
That’s the danger.
Secret sin rarely shows up looking like destruction. It shows up looking like comfort. Like relief. Like one hidden message. One private habit. One compromise nobody will ever see.
But Jesus said it plain: “For nothing is secret that will not be revealed, nor anything hidden that will not be known and come to light.” — Luke 8:17
Not because He wants to shame you.
Because He loves you too much to let darkness become your home.

Sin promises cover.
Then it chains you.
It numbs conviction.
It fractures intimacy with God.
It makes your heart heavy, your prayers cold, and your worship hollow.
But here’s what we miss:
The same light that exposes sin is the same light that heals it.
Jesus does not uncover you to destroy you. He uncovers you to deliver you.

The enemy says, “Hide so you won’t be rejected.”
Jesus says, “Come into the light so you can be restored.”

This is the Gospel: you do not have to keep managing what Christ died to forgive. At the cross, Jesus bore not only your public failures, but the private ones too. The sin nobody knows. The struggle you renamed. The habit you buried. His blood is not weak against hidden things.

Repent.
Come clean before God.
Kill the lie before the lie kills you.

There is mercy for the ashamed.
There is cleansing for the compromised.
There is freedom for the one who is tired of pretending.
Bring it into the light.

Because what stays hidden grows.
But what is surrendered to Jesus can finally die.
And where sin dies, grace begins to breathe again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Stand strong… because hell does not fight empty people.
paragraphs: Stand strong… because hell does not fight empty people.

The enemy does not waste arrows on a man already lying down.
He aims at the one getting up.
The one praying again.
The one choosing purity.
The one refusing to quit.

That is why Ephesians 6 does not tell you to wish.
It tells you to put on the whole armor of God.

Because this battle is real.
Not always loud.
Not always visible.
But real.

Some battles look like temptation.
Some sound like anxiety at 2 a.m.
Some wear the face of shame, fear, compromise, addiction, and silent exhaustion.
But here’s what we miss…
God never called you to fight naked.

He gave you truth when lies feel louder.
He gave you righteousness when the accuser whispers your past.
He gave you the gospel of peace when your heart is shaking.
He gave you the shield of faith to quench flaming darts.
He gave you the helmet of salvation to guard your mind.
And He placed the sword of the Spirit in your hand — the living Word of God.
(Ephesians 6:10–18)

This is not motivational talk.
This is survival.

You do not stand strong because you are naturally fearless.
You stand strong because Christ has already won.

Jesus faced the darkness, bore the curse, crushed sin at the cross, and rose in victory.
So now the believer does not fight for victory.
We fight from victory.
Listen to me, kapatid:

If you are tired, wear the armor.
If you are tempted, wear the armor.
If your mind is under siege, wear the armor.
If you have fallen, repent, rise, and wear the armor again.

The armor of God is not for perfect people.
It is for surrendered people.

Stand strong today.
Not in your own strength.
In the Lord.
In His mighty power.
“Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.” — Ephesians 6:11
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: How Faith Is Actually Built — Romans 10:17
paragraphs: How Faith Is Actually Built — Romans 10:17

Faith is not built by vibes.
It is built by voice.
That is the shock of Romans 10:17.
“So then faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.”

Not by hype.
Not by feelings.
Not by personality.
By the Word.
We keep begging God for stronger faith while starving ourselves of the very thing that creates it.

Open Bible, closed heart? Nothing changes.
Busy church life, no real hearing? Still empty.
Motivational quotes cannot carry what only Scripture can birth.
But here’s what we miss.

Faith is not something you manufacture with mental strain.
Faith is not you trying harder to believe.
Faith is born when Christ speaks through His Word and your soul finally stops arguing long enough to listen.

That means your faith is not built on your mood.
It is built on God’s mouth.

When the enemy whispers,
when shame accuses,
when fear rattles your bones,
you do not need a softer lie.
You need a stronger voice.
And that voice is the Gospel.

You were dead in sin.
Christ came near.
Christ lived the righteousness you could not live.
Christ died the death your guilt deserved.
Christ rose in victory.
And now, through His Word, He calls sinners to repent, believe, and live.
That is how faith is built.

Again and again.
Hearing Christ.
Trusting Christ.
Following Christ.
So if your faith feels weak today, do not panic.

Go back to the Word.
Sit under it.
Read it slowly.
Hear it preached.
Speak it over your trembling soul.
Because weak faith in a strong Christ is still saving faith.
And Jesus is not nervous about your weakness.
He knows how to build what He commands.

Faith grows where Christ’s Word is welcomed.
That is the pathway.
That is the pattern.
That is the mercy of God.

Don’t just chase inspiration.
Hear Him.

Romans 10:17 is not a slogan.
It is a lifeline.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Meaning Behind “Why Are You Looking for the Living Among the Dead?” — Luke 24:5
paragraphs: The Meaning Behind “Why Are You Looking for the Living Among the Dead?” — Luke 24:5
They came looking for a body.

Grief in their hands.
Spices in their arms.
Hope… already buried.
And then heaven interrupts the funeral:
“Why are you looking for the living among the dead?” — Luke 24:5
Pause.

That question wasn’t just for the women at the tomb.
It’s for us.
Because we do this all the time.

We search for life…
in dead relationships.
in secret sin.
in empty success.
in habits that slowly bury our soul.
We go back to what God already called “over.”
But here’s what we miss—
Jesus is not where you left Him.

He is not in your past failure.
He is not in that grave you keep revisiting.
He is not in the shame you keep replaying.
He is risen.
And that changes everything.

The angels didn’t just correct their location—
they exposed a mindset:
You don’t look for resurrection in places of decay.
You don’t find eternal life in temporary things.
You don’t meet a living Savior by clinging to dead chapters.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because the same Jesus they thought was gone…
was already ahead of them.

Alive.
Victorious.
Calling them forward.

Some scholars interpret this moment as both a rebuke and an invitation—
a gentle correction wrapped in divine hope.

“Stop searching there.
Start following Me.”
So let me ask you—

Where are you still looking for life…
in something God already buried?

That addiction?
That toxic cycle?
That version of you that died at the cross?
Let it go.

The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It’s resurrection.

Jesus didn’t come to decorate your grave.
He came to empty it.

Sin was paid for.
Death was defeated.
And through Christ alone, you are invited into real, living hope.
Not someday.
Now.
Come back to the empty tomb.
He’s not there.
He’s alive—and He’s calling you out of the grave too.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 5 Types of Speech That Destroy Relationships
paragraphs: 5 Types of Speech That Destroy Relationships

They didn’t cheat overnight.
They spoke it into existence.

Little words.
Sharp tone.
Careless sentences.
And suddenly… love feels like war.
Listen.

Not all destruction screams.
Some of it whispers daily.
Here are 5 types of speech that quietly kill relationships—and what God says about them:

1. The Knife of Harsh Words
“Why are you like this?”
“You never change.”

It cuts deeper than you admit.
Scripture says, “The tongue has the power of life and death.” (Proverbs 18:21)

You’re not just talking.
You’re planting seeds.

2. The Poison of Constant Criticism
Correction without love becomes condemnation.

You stop seeing a person—
and start attacking a problem.

But here’s what we miss…
Jesus corrects, yes—
but He restores first.

3. The Silence That Punishes
Not peace.
Not wisdom.
Cold silence meant to control.
It says: “You don’t deserve my voice.”

But love doesn’t withdraw to manipulate.
Christ didn’t go silent on you when you failed.
He spoke mercy.

4. The Fire of Gossip & Comparison
“Why can’t you be like…?”
“I heard this about you…”

Comparison kills identity.
Gossip poisons trust.

James 3 calls the tongue a fire—
and some homes are already burning.

5. The Curse of Negative Declarations
“This will never work.”
“You’ll never change.”
“We’re done.”
Careful.

You’re prophesying destruction
over something God might still be healing.
And here’s where grace walks in…

You’ve said things you regret.
We all have.

But Jesus didn’t die just for your actions—
He died for your words too.

On the cross, He absorbed every careless sentence…
