Right on heaven’s clock. At the cross, grace broke into our delay, and through His resurrection, our hope became sure. So when purpose takes time, cling first not to your plan—but to your Savior.

Because your purpose is not ultimately about your platform.
It is about His glory.

Hold on.
Stay faithful.
Keep praying.
Keep obeying.
What God has written over your life will not fail.
Purpose takes time. But Jesus is worth the wait.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Prophet Who Was Fed by Ravens
paragraphs: The Prophet Who Was Fed by Ravens
1 Kings 17:4–6
You thought the wilderness meant God forgot you.
But Elijah learned something beside a dried-up brook:
God can command what cannot be controlled.

“I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there.”
— 1 Kings 17:4
Ravens.
Unclean birds.
Wild birds.
Birds that normally take food—not bring it.
But when God gives the command, even ravens become servants of providence.
God saw it.
You knew.
You were looking at the brook drying up, thinking provision was ending. But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The brook was never Elijah’s source.
God was.
Read that again.

Your job is not your source.
Your strength is not your source.
Your plan is not your source.
Your reputation is not your source.
Jesus Christ is the One who sustains the soul.

“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.”
— Matthew 4:4
Elijah had to obey before he understood.
He had to hide before he was revealed.
He had to depend before he could confront.
And maybe that is where you are.

Dry place.
Hidden place.
Lonely place.
Uncomfortable place.
But not abandoned.

Sin tells you to panic.
Pride tells you to control.
Fear tells you God is late.
But grace says, “Look again.”
The ravens are coming.

Not because Elijah earned it.
Not because he was strong.
But because God is faithful.
And the greater Elijah has already come—Jesus Christ—who entered the wilderness, faced temptation, carried our sin, died on the cross, and rose again so rebels could be redeemed.
Repent.
Trust Christ.
Stop worshiping the brook.
Follow the God who commands ravens.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They nailed it above His head… but most people never read it.
paragraphs: They nailed it above His head… but most people never read it.
“JESUS OF NAZARETH, KING OF THE JEWS.” — written in Latin language, Greek language, and Hebrew language (John 19:19–20).

Three languages.
One message.
But here’s the tension…

It was meant to mock Him.
To shame Him.
To reduce the Son of God into a public joke.
A dying “king.”

Rejected.
Bleeding.
Crowned with thorns instead of gold.
And yet—
That sign was the most honest statement in Jerusalem that day.

Pilate wrote it as sarcasm.
Heaven declared it as truth.

Because while the crowd saw a criminal…
God saw a King taking His throne through a cross.
But here’s what most people miss:

That sign wasn’t just information.
It was invitation.

Latin — the language of power.
Greek — the language of intellect.
Hebrew — the language of religion.

Power.
Philosophy.
Faith.
All confronted with one question:
What will you do with this King?

Not just admire Him.
Not just analyze Him.
Not just debate Him.
Bow… or walk away.

Because the cross is not decoration.
It’s a decision.

Some scholars interpret Pilate’s wording as political mockery to provoke the Jews.
But God turned it into a billboard of salvation.

A King who doesn’t conquer by killing—
but by dying for His enemies.
That includes you.
Yes, you.

Your hidden sin.
Your quiet shame.
Your double life.
He saw it… and still chose the cross.
And the sign above Him still speaks:
This is your King.

Not forcing you.
Not begging you.
But offering you something no crown on earth can give—

forgiveness.
new life.
eternal hope.
So don’t just read the sign.
Respond to it.

From scandal to grace—
because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… boldness replaced fear after the Holy Spirit came?
paragraphs: Did you know… boldness replaced fear after the Holy Spirit came?
They were hiding… then suddenly, they were unshakable.

Before the fire fell, they locked the doors.
Afraid.
Silent.
Watching their backs.

This is the same group that walked with Jesus.
Saw miracles.
Heard His voice.
But still… fear owned them.
Then Pentecost happened.

Wind.
Fire.
Presence.
And everything changed.

Acts of the Apostles 1:8 wasn’t just a promise anymore—
it became power.

Peter the Apostle, who once denied Jesus to a servant girl,
now stands before crowds—
and preaches Christ without flinching.

No filter.
No fear.
No retreat.
What happened?
The Holy Spirit didn’t just comfort them—He transformed them.
But here’s what we miss…

Boldness wasn’t personality.
It wasn’t hype.
It wasn’t self-confidence.
It was Christ alive in them.

Because when the Spirit fills you,
you stop protecting your image—
and start proclaiming His name.

Fear says: “Stay quiet.”
The Spirit says: “Speak life.”

Fear says: “You’ll lose everything.”
The Spirit says: “In Christ, you already gained everything.”

And that same Spirit?
He hasn’t changed.

2 Timothy 1:7 says:
God did not give you a spirit of fear—
but of power, love, and a sound mind.

So if fear is still leading…
maybe surrender hasn’t finished yet.
But here’s the good news—

Jesus doesn’t just forgive your fear.
He replaces it.

At the cross, He took your shame.
In the resurrection, He secured your victory.
And through the Spirit, He gives you boldness to live it out.

This isn’t about becoming loud.
It’s about becoming alive in Christ.
So today—

Step out.
Speak up.
Stand firm.
Not because you’re strong…
But because He is in you.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Born again through the Spirit — John 3
paragraphs: Born again through the Spirit — John 3
He was religious.

Respected.
Moral.
Educated.

And Jesus still told him, “You must be born again.”
Not improved.
Not polished.
Born again.
That is the shock of John 3.

Nicodemus came to Jesus with status, knowledge, and questions. But Jesus went straight to the wound beneath the religion: flesh cannot produce spirit. Human effort cannot create divine life. Church attendance cannot resurrect a dead heart. Good behavior cannot make a sinner new.
“But here’s what we miss…”

Jesus was not shaming Nicodemus. He was exposing the mercy of God. The new birth is not something you achieve. It is something the Spirit performs. You cannot manufacture salvation. You must receive it. “That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).
This is the Gospel.

We were not just misguided. We were dead in sin. And dead people do not need inspiration. They need resurrection. That is why Jesus came. He would go from that midnight conversation to a bloody cross, bearing the judgment we deserved, so that all who believe in Him would not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16). The Spirit gives new birth because the Son gave His life.
So hear this, beloved:

You do not need a better mask.
You need a new heart.
You do not need spiritual cosmetics.
You need spiritual life.
And in Christ, that miracle is real.

No past is too filthy.
No heart is too cold.
No sinner is too far gone.
The same Spirit who causes the wind to move where it wills can breathe life into you today. Repent. Believe in Jesus. Be made new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: It doesn’t shout.
paragraphs: It doesn’t shout.
It doesn’t flex.
Sometimes… pride kneels.
And you still don’t see it.
4 Ways Pride Disguises Itself as Strength

1. “I don’t need help.”
You call it independence.
God calls it isolation.

You carry everything alone, refusing correction, dodging accountability.
But Scripture cuts through the lie: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Strength isn’t refusing help.
Strength is knowing you need God—and letting others in.

2. “I’m just being honest.”
No… you’re being harsh.

You weaponize truth without love.
You speak facts, but leave wounds.

“But here’s what we miss…”
Truth without grace is not Christlike.

Jesus was full of both (John 1:14).
If your honesty crushes more than it heals, pride is wearing your voice.

3. “I know what I’m doing.”
Confidence feels powerful—until it ignores God.

You stop praying.
Stop seeking.
Start assuming.

Proverbs 16:18 doesn’t whisper—it warns:
“Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.”

The fall doesn’t start with failure.
It starts with self-sufficiency.

4. “I’ve changed—I’m better now.”
Growth is good.
But pride sneaks in when you start taking the credit.

You forget the nights God carried you.
The mercy that covered you.
The cross that saved you.

And just like that…
grace becomes background noise.
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because pride builds a throne…
…but Jesus carried a cross.

Jesus Christ didn’t cling to power—He humbled Himself to death (Philippians 2:8).
Not because He was weak.
Because love chose surrender.
So if this hits deep—don’t defend it.
Lay it down.

Pride says, “I’ve got this.”
Grace says, “Come to Me.”
And only one of those saves you.

From hidden pride to open surrender—
because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most People Miss This About Shame Entering the Story
paragraphs: Most People Miss This About Shame Entering the Story
They didn’t just eat the fruit.
They felt something break.

Silence fell.
Eyes opened.
And suddenly—they saw themselves.

Naked.
Exposed.
Uncovered.
That’s when shame entered the story.

Not when God spoke.
Not when judgment came.
But the moment sin twisted their vision.
“Then the eyes of both were opened… and they knew that they were naked.” (Genesis 3:7)
Catch this.

Before sin—no hiding.
After sin—covering.
They stitched fig leaves like bandages on a wound they couldn’t name.
And we’ve been doing the same ever since.

Different leaves.
Same shame.

Success to hide insecurity.
Filters to hide identity.
Silence to hide sin.
But here’s what we miss…
God didn’t walk away.
He walked toward them.
“Where are you?”

Not because He didn’t know.
But because they were lost in shame.
And here’s the holy tension—

The first question God asks fallen humanity
is not “What did you do?”
It’s “Where are you?”

Location before accusation.
Heart before behavior.
That’s grace… before the cross even appears.
But God doesn’t leave them in fig leaves.

He replaces their fragile covering
with something stronger.
Garments of skin. (Genesis 3:21)

Something had to die
to cover their shame.
That’s not random.
That’s a whisper of the Gospel.

Because one day,
Jesus Christ
would step into our nakedness…
take our shame…
and be stripped so we could be covered.

Not with leaves.
But with righteousness.
You’re not hiding from God.
You’re hiding because of shame.
And He’s still asking—
“Where are you?”

Not to expose you.
But to restore you.

Come out of the shadows.
Drop the leaves.
Let grace cover what shame tried to define.
Someone you know is still hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 🚨 MOST PEOPLE SAY THEY HAVE FAITH…
paragraphs:
🚨 MOST PEOPLE SAY THEY HAVE FAITH…
…but their life never changes.
Let’s be honest.

You say you trust God…
but you keep delaying obedience.
You hear the Word…
but you don’t act on it.

That’s not faith.
That’s comfort disguised as belief.
And it’s keeping you stuck.
(For serious believers only)
This is not a motivational read.
This is a wake-up call.

This book will confront the lie that you can believe in God…
without actually following Him.

It will challenge your comfort.
Expose your excuses.
And call you into real obedience.
🔥 INSIDE THIS BOOK, YOU’LL DISCOVER:

• Why faith without action is spiritually dangerous
• The hidden reason you keep delaying obedience
• How to break out of passive Christianity
• What real biblical faith actually looks like
• Why grace empowers obedience—not excuses sin
• How to move when God speaks (even when it’s uncomfortable)
⚔️ THIS IS WHERE MOST PEOPLE GET EXPOSED

Most people say “I believe in God”
Few actually obey Him

Most people wait for the perfect moment
Few move when God says “now”

Most people want blessings
Few want surrender

Most people stay comfortable
Few step out of the boat
Which one are you?
🔒 THIS IS NOT FOR EVERYONE
This book is NOT public.
This is a growing movement of believers who are done with:

• Lukewarm faith
• Excuses and delay
• Empty Christianity
• Spiritual inconsistency
And are serious about:

• Obedience
• Discipline
• Real transformation
• Following Jesus for real
⚡ THIS IS YOUR MOMENT

If you feel convicted right now…
that’s not pressure.
That’s God calling you higher.

Stop waiting.
Stop delaying.
Stop pretending.
Step into a faith that actually moves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When Jesus died on the cross, His last words were clear:
paragraphs: When Jesus died on the cross, His last words were clear:
“It is finished.” (John 19:30)

Finished.
Not pending.
Not “to be completed in hell.”
Finished.
So what happened next?

Jesus’ body was laid in the tomb.
But His spirit—listen carefully—did not go to suffer in hell.
He said to the thief beside Him:
“Today you will be with Me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43)

Not tomorrow.
Not after a battle in hell.
Today.
Paradise.
But here’s where people get confused…
There’s a verse:
“He descended into the lower parts of the earth.” (Ephesians 4:9)
Some interpret this as hell.
But many scholars explain this as Jesus entering the realm of the dead (sometimes called Hades), not the place of eternal punishment (Gehenna).
And He didn’t go there as a victim.
He went as Victor.
Then comes this powerful line:
“I hold the keys of death and Hades.” (Revelation 1:18)
Keys mean authority.

Not that Jesus had to fight demons to get them—
but that through the cross and resurrection,
He claimed absolute authority over death itself.
So did Jesus go to hell to suffer?
No.
He already bore the full wrath of sin on the cross.
Did He descend to the dead?

Yes—
not to be defeated,
but to declare:
“It’s done.”
And here’s where grace hits you.
Hard.

You don’t have to go to hell
to prove your worth.

Jesus already went through death
so you could walk in life.

Sin had a key.
Death had a grip.
Hell had a claim.
But Jesus…
took it all.
And now?
The door is open.

Not because you’re good—
but because He is.
Because clarity leads to freedom.
And freedom has a name.
Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He worked with his hands… so no one could question his heart.
paragraphs: He worked with his hands… so no one could question his heart.
That’s the tension.
The apostle Paul the Apostle—a preacher carrying eternity in his mouth—still chose to carry leather, tools, and sweat in his hands.
Not because ministry wasn’t worthy of support.
But because people were watching.
“I have not coveted anyone’s silver or gold or clothing.” — Acts 20:33
And again:
“You yourselves know that these hands of mine have supplied my own needs…” — Acts 20:34
He was a tentmaker.
Quiet.
Hidden.
Honest work.
But don’t miss this—
Paul wasn’t saying ministers shouldn’t be supported.
In fact, he clearly taught the opposite:
“The Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 9:14
So why did he refuse it sometimes?
Here’s the piercing truth:

He would rather suffer loss…
than let anyone mistake the Gospel for a business.
That’s where it hits.
Hard.

Because today, it’s easy to mix calling with comfort…
anointing with ambition…
ministry with money.
But Paul drew a line.
Sharp.
Clear.
Costly.
“I won’t let silver compete with souls.”
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because this isn’t about condemning provision.
It’s about examining motive.
Why do we serve?
Why do we preach?
Why do we give?
Jesus didn’t die for profit.
He bled for people.

And the Gospel is still free—
even if it costs us everything to carry it.
Ask yourself:
“Would I still serve… if no one paid me?”
And if your answer trembles—
Run back to the cross.
Because in Christ, we don’t serve for gain.
We serve because we’ve already been given everything.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most People Miss This Detail in God Seeing Leah
paragraphs: Most People Miss This Detail in God Seeing Leah

She wasn’t unloved.
She was unseen.
And most people miss that.
We read the story of Leah and rush to label her: the unwanted wife… the second choice… the one Jacob didn’t desire.
But that’s not the detail that should shake you.
It’s this:
God didn’t just notice her pain—He named it.
“When the Lord saw that Leah was hated…” (Genesis 29:31)
Saw.

Not glanced at.
Not overlooked.
Saw.

Her silent tears.
Her forced marriage.
Her aching comparison to her sister.
And then—God did something scandalous.
He opened her womb.

Not Rachel’s.
Leah’s.
The rejected one became fruitful.
But here’s what we miss…

Leah didn’t start with worship.
She started with longing.

“Now my husband will love me…”
“Now he will be attached to me…”

Her early prayers weren’t pure.
They were desperate.
Relatable, right?

We don’t always come to God clean.
We come needy.
And God still listens.
But watch the shift.
By her fourth son, everything changes:
“This time I will praise the Lord.” (Genesis 29:35)

No mention of Jacob.
No chasing approval.
Just… praise.
And that son?
Judah.
From his bloodline would come Jesus Christ.
Let that land.

The woman who felt invisible
became part of the line that would reveal God in the flesh.
That’s grace.

Not because she had it all together—
but because God sees what others ignore.

So if you feel overlooked…
second place…
never chosen…
He sees you.

Not the filtered version.
Not the strong version.
You.
And He doesn’t just see.
He redeems.
He rewrites.

He brings purpose out of pain—
and glory out of rejection.
God never overlooks the unloved.
He builds legacies through them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most People Miss This About Working 14 Years for Rachel
paragraphs: Most People Miss This About Working 14 Years for Rachel
He worked 14 years… and still didn’t get what he thought he was promised.
Let that sit.
Jacob loved Rachel so deeply that Scripture says “they seemed like only a few days to him because of his love for her” (see Genesis 29:20).
Sounds romantic.
But most people miss the tension.

He was deceived.
Delayed.
Denied.

First 7 years—he gets tricked into marrying Leah.
Another 7 years—he keeps working for Rachel.
Fourteen years of labor… for one promise.
Here’s what we miss:
Love didn’t make it easy. It made it worth enduring.
Jacob’s story is not just about romance.
It’s about transformation.
This is the same man who once manipulated his brother, lied to his father, and ran from consequences. Now?

He’s learning to wait.
To serve.
To be refined through delay.
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because sometimes God allows long seasons not to punish you… but to reshape you.
Some scholars interpret this passage as a cultural marriage arrangement story. But Scripture reveals something deeper:
God was not just giving Jacob a wife.
He was forming a man.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.

Working.
Waiting.
Wondering why it’s taking so long.
Listen carefully:

Jesus didn’t come just to give you what you want.
He came to redeem who you are.
At the cross, Christ didn’t wait 14 years—He gave His life in full, for sinners like us. No deception. No delay. Just grace poured out.
Your waiting is not wasted.
In Christ, your story is not stuck—it’s being rewritten.
So if you’re in a “14-year season”…
Don’t quit.
God is doing deeper work than you can see.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… distractions often appear when purpose is near?
paragraphs: Did you know… distractions often appear when purpose is near?
It shows up right when you start getting serious.

Not random.
Not accidental.
Strategic.

You finally decide to pray deeper—suddenly your phone feels louder.
You commit to purity—temptation sharpens its voice.
You step toward purpose—old habits start knocking like they still own the house.
Why?

Because distraction isn’t just noise.
It’s often resistance.

Even Nehemiah felt this.
When he was rebuilding the wall, enemies kept calling him away—
“Come down. Let’s talk.”
But his answer?
“I am doing a great work and I cannot come down.” (Nehemiah 6:3)
That’s the posture.
But here’s what we miss…
Distraction only fights what has direction.

The enemy doesn’t waste time on empty lives.
He targets movement. Calling. Alignment with God.

So if everything suddenly feels harder—
focus slipping, discipline shaking, noise increasing—
It might not mean you’re failing.
It might mean you’re close.

Close to breakthrough.
Close to obedience.
Close to becoming the person God called you to be.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because you won’t win this by willpower alone.
You win by surrender.

Hebrews says:
“Let us throw off everything that hinders… and run with perseverance.”

Not walk.
Run.

Eyes fixed on Jesus—
the One who ignored every distraction of this world…
even the cross’s shame…
for the joy of redeeming you.
Listen.

Your purpose is not fragile.
But your focus needs guarding.

So don’t entertain what God told you to escape.
Don’t negotiate with what Jesus already defeated.
Lift your eyes again.

You’re not losing ground.
You’re being refined in the fire of resistance.

And in Christ—
you will not come down.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Are you starving your spirit while feeding every other appetite?
paragraphs: Are you starving your spirit while feeding every other appetite?
That’s the danger.

We scroll for hours.
We binge opinions.
We consume noise like it’s nourishment.
But Jesus said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.” — Matthew 4:4

That means a full stomach can still hide an empty soul.
A busy life can still be spiritually malnourished.
A smiling face can still cover a starving faith.
And here’s what we miss:

Faith does not grow by accident.
It must be fed.

Not with hype.
Not with vibes.
Not with borrowed convictions from someone else’s sermon clip.
It is fed by the Word of God.

When temptation hits, Jesus did not fight Satan with feelings.
He fought with Scripture.
Not because He was weak.
Because He was showing us where real strength comes from.
Some of us are trying to survive spiritual battles on snack-sized devotion and leftover Sunday faith.

No wonder we feel dry.
No wonder we fold so quickly.
No wonder anxiety gets loud when truth gets quiet.
But grace walks in here.

Jesus is not just telling you to read the Bible more.
He is calling you back to life.
Back to truth.
Back to the voice that heals what sin, fear, and shame have been feeding.

Feed your faith, and your flesh stops leading.
Feed your faith, and your mind starts clearing.
Feed your faith, and Christ becomes bigger than the craving, the fear, the failure.

Open the Word.
Read it slow.
Chew on it.
Pray it back.
Live it out.
Because your soul was never designed to live on bread alone.
It was made for Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Joseph’s Coat Being Stripped
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Joseph’s Coat Being Stripped
(Genesis 37:23)
They took his coat.
Not his calling.
Genesis 37:23 says Joseph’s brothers “stripped Joseph of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him.”
Read that again.

They could remove what marked him.
They could mock what favored him.
They could throw him into a pit.
But they could not cancel what God had spoken.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.

You were stripped of trust.
Stripped of dignity.
Stripped of family support.
Stripped of the version of life you thought you would have.
And the enemy whispered, “Now you are nothing.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
A stripped coat is not a stripped destiny.
Joseph lost the garment, but not the God who gave the dream.
God saw it.
You knew the betrayal hurt deeper because it came from people close enough to recognize your coat.

But Genesis 50:20 gives the reveal:
“You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good.”
That is the Gospel pattern.
Jesus was also stripped.
“They stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe.” (Matthew 27:28)
The innocent Son of God was shamed publicly, nailed brutally, and crushed for sinners like us.
Not because we were good.
Because we were guilty.

Sin stripped us of righteousness.
Pride stripped us of truth.
Rebellion stripped us of life with God.
But Jesus took the shame so grace could cover us.
“By grace are ye saved through faith… not of works.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)
So repent.

Stop clinging to the coat they took.
Come to Christ, who gives a robe no enemy can remove.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They followed a homeless Rabbi…
paragraphs:
They followed a homeless Rabbi…
but somehow, the mission never lacked.

Food appeared.
Travel happened.
Needs were met.
So who was really financing Jesus?
Here’s the part many people skip.
It wasn’t kings. Not Rome. Not the temple system.
It was… transformed lives.
📖 Luke 8:2–3 opens the curtain:
“Joanna… Susanna, and many others were contributing to their support out of their own means.”
Let that sink in.
Women—healed, restored, set free—became partners in the mission.
The Hidden Treasury

Among them was Joanna, connected to Herod’s household.
Influence.

There was Mary Magdalene, once bound by demons.
Deliverance.

There were “many others.”
Unnamed. Unseen. But not unnoticed by heaven.
They gave from their own resources.

Not leftovers.
Not obligation.
Gratitude turned into generosity.
And there’s more…
Jesus also had a money bag, carried by Judas Iscariot (John 12:6).
Which means:

There was structure.
There was stewardship.
There was giving happening regularly.
Even if one of the carriers had a broken heart.
But here’s what we miss…
Jesus never begged.
He never manipulated.
He never built His mission on pressure.
He built it on transformation.

People who encountered grace
couldn’t help but support the mission of grace.
The deeper truth

God financed His Son’s ministry
through people whose lives were changed by that same Son.

Not obligation.
Overflow.
And that still hasn’t changed.

The Gospel moves forward today
on the backs of people who remember
who they used to be…
and who Jesus made them now.

So the real question isn’t just:
“Who financed Jesus?”
It’s this:
Has His grace moved you enough to become part of the mission?
Someone needs to hear this.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 6 Truths About Who You Are in God
paragraphs: 6 Truths About Who You Are in God
You don’t even know who you are.

And that confusion?
It’s costing you your calling.

You keep introducing yourself by your past.
God introduces you by your redemption.
Let me remind you—not hype, not feelings, but truth rooted in Scripture.

1. You are chosen.
Not random. Not accidental.
“Before I formed you… I knew you.” (Jeremiah 1:5)
God didn’t pick you last—He picked you on purpose.

2. You are forgiven.
Yes, that sin.
Yes, the one you replay at 2AM.
“In Him we have redemption through His blood.” (Ephesians 1:7)
The cross didn’t miss a spot.

3. You are a new creation.
Not improved. Not repaired.
New.
“Anyone in Christ is a new creation.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
Stop wearing graves like they’re clothes.

4. You are God’s child.
Not just a believer—family.
“To all who received Him… He gave the right to become children of God.” (John 1:12)
You don’t beg for love—you belong to it.

5. You are empowered.
Not weak. Not helpless.
“The same Spirit… lives in you.” (Romans 8:11)
You’re carrying resurrection power in ordinary skin.

6. You are sent.
This is where most people shrink back.
But Jesus said, “As the Father has sent Me, I am sending you.” (John 20:21)
You’re not just saved—you’re commissioned.
But here’s what we miss…
You can know all of this—and still live like a slave.

Because identity isn’t just learned.
It’s received.
And that happens at the feet of Jesus.

So today—drop the false names.
Failure. Addict. Not enough. Too late.

That’s not your voice.
That’s not your Father.
Jesus rewrote your identity in His blood.
And He’s not taking it back.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most People Miss This About Judah Suggesting the Sale
paragraphs: Most People Miss This About Judah Suggesting the Sale

He didn’t throw the stone.
He made a deal.
That’s what most people miss about Judah suggesting they sell Joseph in Book of Genesis 37.

It looks like mercy.
But it was still betrayal.

“Why kill him?” Judah says.
“Let’s profit from him.”
Pause.

That’s not compassion.
That’s calculated sin dressed as wisdom.

He spared Joseph’s life—
but still crushed his destiny… or so it seemed.
And here’s the uncomfortable truth:

Some of us don’t destroy people outright.
We just compromise them.

We don’t pull the trigger—
we just sign the deal.

We don’t “hate”—
we just justify.
But here’s what we miss…

God was not absent in that pit.
He was writing a bigger story.

Joseph’s chains became the pathway to purpose.
The betrayal became the bridge to salvation for many.
And Judah?

The same Judah who sold his brother…
would later offer himself as a substitute for Benjamin (Genesis 44).

That’s not coincidence.
That’s redemption.

And generations later—
from Judah’s bloodline—came Jesus Christ.
The Lion of Judah.
Let that sink in.

The man who sold his brother…
became part of the lineage of the Savior who would be sold for us.
That’s the Gospel.

We are all Judah.
We’ve all traded truth for convenience.
Chose profit over purity.
Silence over righteousness.
But Jesus—

He steps into our story.
Takes the price of our betrayal.
And offers mercy we never earned.

Not a deal.
A cross.

So if you’ve compromised…
if you’ve justified…
if you’ve been the one who “didn’t kill—but still hurt”—
Grace is still calling your name.

Repent.
Return.
Be rewritten.

Because God doesn’t cancel Judahs.
He redeems them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Not every opportunity is from God (1 Corinthians 10:23)
paragraphs: Not every opportunity is from God (1 Corinthians 10:23)
Not every open door came from God.

Some doors are profitable.
Some are exciting.
Some are legal.
Some are applauded.
But still not holy.
“Everything is permissible,” Paul wrote, “but not everything is beneficial… not everything builds up” (1 Corinthians 10:23).
That changes everything.

Because the question is not only, Can I do this?
The deeper question is, Will this draw me closer to Christ, or slowly pull me away?

The enemy does not always tempt with obvious evil.
Sometimes he offers a polished opportunity.
A bigger platform.
A faster paycheck.
A relationship that feels right.
A shortcut that looks harmless.

But here’s what we miss:
Not every blessing-looking thing is from the hand of God.
Some opportunities feed the flesh while starving the soul.

God is not just leading you into what is available.
He is leading you into what is obedient.

So before you say yes, pray.
Before you move, weigh it by Scripture.
Before you call it favor, ask whether it produces holiness, peace, and faithfulness.
Because a good opportunity can still become a bad decision when Jesus is not Lord over it.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Maybe you said yes too quickly.
Maybe you chased what glittered.
Maybe you called compromise “wisdom.”

Come back.
Christ does not shame the repentant.
He restores them.

Jesus is still able to redirect your steps, redeem your wrong turns, and teach your heart to desire what truly builds. His will is not a prison. It is protection. His commands are not chains. They are life.

So do not chase every open door.
Chase the Shepherd.
He still knows the way.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 🚨 WHAT IF YOUR FEAR IS THE ONLY THING DISOBEYING GOD?
paragraphs: 🚨 WHAT IF YOUR FEAR IS THE ONLY THING DISOBEYING GOD?

Not your weakness.
Not your past.
Not your lack of clarity.
Your fear.

You keep saying:
“I just don’t want to mess it up.”

But what if that thought…
is the very thing keeping you stuck?

You’re waiting for certainty.
God is waiting for obedience.
“What If I Mess It Up? Trusting God Anyway”
This is not a soft encouragement book.
This will confront you.
Because deep down—you already know what God told you to do.
You just haven’t moved.
🔥 THIS BOOK WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE OBEDIENCE
Inside, you’ll discover:

• Why fear of failure is actually a form of control
• How perfectionism is silently killing your faith
• What to do when you actually mess up
• How to move forward without full clarity
• Why God’s grace is bigger than your worst mistake
• The mindset shift that turns hesitation into bold action
⚔️ HERE’S THE TRUTH MOST PEOPLE WON’T ACCEPT

Most people want God’s will…
but only if it feels safe.
Few people obey when it feels risky.

Most people delay until they feel ready.
Few people move when God speaks.

Most people stay stuck in “what if.”
Few people step into “even if.”
🚪 THIS IS NOT FOR EVERYONE

It’s not for casual readers.
It’s for believers who are DONE playing safe.
Inside the library:

• Daily faith-strengthening content
• Real discipleship—not motivation
• Constant new releases being added
This is a movement of disciplined, obedient believers.
⚡ WHO ARE YOU BECOMING?
The one who keeps hesitating?
Or the one who obeys—even when afraid?
Unlock this book and step into bold, fearless faith:
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Anxiety is loud.
paragraphs:
Anxiety is loud.
But God does not whisper back with panic.

Philippians 4:6–7 (KJV)
“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.”

Here’s the shock of the text: Paul does not say, pretend nothing hurts. He says, bring everything to God.
Not some things.
Everything.

The pressure.
The fear.
The secret exhaustion behind the smile.

And here’s where grace walks in: the promise is not that every problem disappears overnight. The promise is that God’s peace will stand guard over your heart and mind through Christ Jesus. That means panic does not get the final word. Jesus does.

Prayer is not denial.
It is surrender.
Thanksgiving is not fake positivity.
It is faith remembering that God has been faithful before.

So when your mind is racing, do not run first to despair. Run to the Father. Pour it out. Name it. Cry if you must. But pray. And the peace of God—deeper than logic, stronger than emotion—will hold you together when life tries to tear you apart.

Hope in Christ:
Jesus carried the full weight of our sin and sorrow at the cross, and because of Him, we are not abandoned in our anxiety. We are invited into peace. Real peace. Holy peace. Guarding peace.

Prayer:
Lord Jesus, my heart is heavy and my thoughts are restless. I bring everything to You. Teach me to pray instead of panic, to thank You instead of drowning in fear, and to rest in the peace only You can give. Amen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Is Risen… Now What? — Colossians 3:1
paragraphs: He Is Risen… Now What? — Colossians 3:1
He walked out of the grave.
So why are so many believers still living like they’re buried?
“Since, then, you have been raised with Christ, set your hearts on things above…” — Colossians 3:1
Resurrection is not just a moment we celebrate.
It is a life we step into.

Jesus did not rise so you could stay chained to the same pride, the same secret sin, the same fear, the same old appetite that kept crushing your soul. He rose to pull you into a new way of living. New desires. New direction. New obedience.
But here’s what we miss:
A risen Christ demands a risen life.
You cannot sing about the empty tomb on Sunday and then crawl back into dead things on Monday. Not if you belong to Him. Not if His blood bought you. Not if His Spirit lives in you.
Colossians 3:1 is a summons. Lift your eyes. Set your heart higher. Stop feeding what Jesus came to bury. Start pursuing what He died and rose to give—holiness, purity, mercy, truth, courage, love.
This is not behavior modification.
This is resurrection power.

And when you fail—and sometimes you will—you do not run back to shame. You run to Christ. The same Savior who rose from the grave still receives repentant sinners with nail-scarred hands and unstoppable grace.
So now what?

Now we seek Him.
Now we surrender.
Now we live like the tomb is still empty.
Because it is.

And that means your past does not get the final word.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your guilt does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Training Your Mind for Faith — Philippians 4:8
paragraphs: Training Your Mind for Faith — Philippians 4:8
Your mind is being discipled by whatever you keep replaying.

That is why Philippians 4:8 is not soft advice.
It is spiritual warfare.
“Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable… think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)
Paul knew something we forget: before sin shows up in public, it usually settles in private thoughts first. Fear grows there. Lust grows there. Bitterness grows there. Unbelief grows there.
But so does faith.

Faith is not trained by panic.
Faith is trained by focus.

When your mind keeps feeding on lies, you will live restless. When your thoughts kneel before truth, your soul starts to steady. This is not pretending pain is not real. This is choosing what gets the final word.

And here’s what we miss: Paul is not telling us to think positively just to feel better. He is calling us to think biblically so we can live faithfully. Truth over distortion. Purity over pollution. Beauty over corruption. Christ over chaos.

So when anxiety starts shouting, answer it with what is true.
When temptation starts whispering, answer it with what is pure.
When shame starts choking your heart, answer it with the Gospel.

Because the clearest truth to set your mind on is this: Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose again, and is able to redeem not only your future, but even your thought life. He does not only forgive dirty actions. He renews disordered minds.

Train your mind.
Guard the gate.
Feed your faith.
And when your thoughts wander, do not run from Christ in shame. Run to Him in surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 5 Things You Need to Let Go to Grow
paragraphs: 5 Things You Need to Let Go to Grow
You can’t carry your calling if your hands are full of what’s killing you.
Read that again.

Growth isn’t just about adding more.
It’s about letting go of what God never asked you to hold.
Here are 5 things you need to release—if you’re serious about becoming who God called you to be:

1. The Need to Be Liked by Everyone
Approval can become an idol in disguise.
Even Jesus Christ was rejected—and He was perfect.
You weren’t called to be liked.
You were called to be faithful.

2. Hidden Sin You Keep Justifying
That “small” compromise? It’s not small.
Sin grows in silence.
But grace meets you in confession.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive…” (1 John 1:9)

3. Your Old Identity
Stop introducing yourself by your past.
You are not your failure.
You are not your shame.

In Christ, you are new.
Completely rewritten.

4. Control Over Everything
You’re exhausted because you’re trying to play God.
Let go.

Surrender isn’t weakness.
It’s trust in the One who sees what you can’t.

5. Bitterness You’ve Been Feeding
Unforgiveness feels powerful—until you realize it’s poisoning you.
You don’t heal by holding on.
You heal by releasing.
But here’s what we miss…

Letting go feels like loss—
until you realize you’re making space for grace.

For freedom.
For Christ Himself.

Jesus didn’t die just to improve your life.
He died to transform it.

So today—drop it.
The sin.
The weight.
The fear.
And run to Him.

Because what you let go of in obedience,
God replaces with something eternal.
From burden to breakthrough—because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He carried a calling from God…
paragraphs:
He carried a calling from God…
and blood on his hands.

Not a metaphor.
A real body.
A buried secret in the sand.
Moses wasn’t just a leader-in-waiting—he was a fugitive.
Scripture doesn’t hide it.
In Exodus 2:12, he looks both ways… sees no one… and kills an Egyptian.
Then he hides the body.
That’s the résumé of the man God would use to split seas.
Let that sit.
You think your past disqualifies you?

Moses thought the same.
He ran.
Forty years in obscurity.
Dust. Silence. Regret.
But here’s what we miss…

God didn’t call Moses after he cleaned himself up.
God called him while he was still carrying the weight of what he did.
A burning bush doesn’t erase a bloody past.
Grace does.

When God speaks in Exodus 3, He doesn’t say,
“Moses, prove you’ve changed.”

He says,
“I have seen the suffering… and I am sending you.”
Sending.
A former murderer.
This is the scandal of grace:

God doesn’t build His kingdom with perfect people.
He builds it with surrendered ones.

Yes, sin is real.
Yes, justice matters.
Moses’ act was wrong—no excuses.
But sin doesn’t get the final word.
Jesus does.

Because centuries later, another Deliverer would come—
not with hidden sin…
but to carry ours.

Jesus Christ didn’t bury bodies in the sand—
He was buried for ours.
And then He walked out of the grave.
Alive.

So your past?
It’s not your identity.

Repent.
Turn.
Bring it into the light.

Because the same God who met Moses in the wilderness
meets you right where you are.
Not to shame you—
but to send you.
Someone you know is still running from their past.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re stressing about tomorrow… but Jesus already stepped into it.
paragraphs: You’re stressing about tomorrow… but Jesus already stepped into it.
“Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.” — Matthew 6:34
You feel it, don’t you?

That quiet panic.
The “what ifs.”
The weight of things that haven’t even happened yet.

Bills not paid.
Decisions not made.
Outcomes you can’t control.
And your mind runs ahead… like it’s trying to play God.
But listen—Jesus cuts through the noise with one command:
“Do not worry.”

Not because life is easy.
Not because problems aren’t real.
But because you are not alone in tomorrow.
He already stands there.

We worry because we think everything depends on us.
Provision. Protection. The future.
But here’s what we miss…
Worry is a quiet form of unbelief.

It says:
“God, I trust You for yesterday… but not for what’s next.”
And yet Scripture keeps pulling us back:

The same God who fed you yesterday…
The same Savior who carried your sin on the cross…
The same Spirit who woke you up today…
He will not abandon you tomorrow.
This verse isn’t just about anxiety.
It’s about lordship.
Who’s really in control of your future?

Because when Jesus died and rose again, He didn’t just save your soul—
He claimed your tomorrows.

Your unknowns.
Your fears.
Your unfinished stories.
So breathe.

Not shallow.
Not rushed.
Deep.
Then surrender what hasn’t happened yet.
Give it to the One who already wrote the ending in grace.
Type “I trust You, Lord”—not for show, but as surrender.
Because peace isn’t found in control.
It’s found in Christ.
From anxiety to assurance—because Jesus already stands in your tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.” — Hebrews 6:19
paragraphs: “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.” — Hebrews 6:19

The storm doesn’t ask permission.
It just comes.

Waves of fear.
Winds of doubt.
Nights where your prayers feel like they hit the ceiling and fall back on your chest.
And then this verse whispers—
Anchor.

Not a wish.
Not positive thinking.
Not “baka okay lang.”

Hope.
But not ordinary hope.

This hope is tied to something unshakable—
Jesus Himself, who already went behind the curtain… into the very presence of God.
Back then, only the high priest could enter that place. Once a year. Carefully. Fearfully.
But Jesus?
He didn’t visit.
He secured it.

So when your life feels like it’s drifting—
your future unclear, your heart tired, your faith shaking—
your anchor isn’t in your strength.

It’s already lodged
in Heaven.
But here’s what we miss…
An anchor only works if it’s set deep.

You don’t feel it during calm seas.
You feel it when everything tries to pull you away.

That anxiety?
That hidden sin?
That silent battle you don’t tell anyone?
They’re trying to drag you.
But grace says:
“You’re still held.”

Not because you’re perfect—
but because Jesus already went where you couldn’t
and did what you never could.

He carried your sin.
He tore the veil.
He made a way.
So today—
Don’t just admire the anchor.
Hold on to it.

Repent where you need to repent.
Return where you’ve drifted.
Rest in the One who already secured your place.
Because this hope?

Firm.
Secure.
Unbreakable.
Even when you’re not.
From storm to stillness—because Jesus holds what you cannot.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some doors God closes are actually protection, not punishment (Revelation 3:7)
paragraphs: Some doors God closes are actually protection, not punishment (Revelation 3:7)
The door slammed shut… and you called it rejection.
But heaven called it rescue.

You prayed. You fasted. You knocked until your knuckles bled in silence.
And still—nothing opened.
So you questioned God.

“Why block me?”
“Why now?”
“Why this?”
Then Revelation 3:7 whispers something we often miss:
“What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open.”

Not maybe.
Not sometimes.
No one.
But here’s what we miss…

We celebrate open doors.
We resent closed ones.
Yet some doors are sealed by mercy.

That relationship you begged for?
It would have broken your calling.

That job you cried over?
It would have buried your purpose.

That opportunity that vanished?
It would have cost you your soul.

Closed.
Not to punish you—
but to protect what God placed inside you.

Because God doesn’t just open paths…
He guards destinies.
And if He shut it, it means He saw something you couldn’t.

Danger you didn’t discern.
Pain you weren’t prepared for.
A future that didn’t carry His presence.
So He said no.

Not rejection—
Redirection.

Not denial—
Divine intervention.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Jesus didn’t die just to open doors…
He died to be the door (John 10:9).

Meaning your security is not in opportunities—
It’s in Him.

Even when the way feels blocked,
the cross proves you are never abandoned.
So breathe.

If God closed it,
you don’t need to reopen it.

There’s a better door coming—
one aligned with His will,
covered in His peace,
and marked with His presence.

From shut doors to saved destinies—
because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They nailed Him to wood…
paragraphs:
They nailed Him to wood…
and somehow we turned it into buildings, brands, and boundaries.
Pause.
Did Jesus come to build a religion?
No.
But He did say something that shakes the ground beneath that question:
“I will build My church…” — Matthew 16:18
So what did He mean?

Not a system.
Not an institution.
Not a checklist of rituals to earn God.

The word He used for church was “ekklesia” — a called-out people.
Not walls.
People.
Living. Breathing. Broken people.

Like you.
Like me.
Here’s where we miss it—

Religion says: Clean yourself, then come.
Jesus says: Come, and I’ll make you clean.

Religion builds ladders to heaven.
Jesus brought heaven down—through His blood, through His cross.
And yes, over time, people organized. Structures formed. Traditions grew. Some beautiful. Some… heavy.
Some scholars interpret that the early followers naturally gathered into communities with leaders and practices (see Acts 2). That’s not wrong.
But hear this clearly:

Jesus didn’t die to create a system you perform for.
He died to restore a relationship you were made for.

The “church” He builds is not made of concrete.
It’s made of redeemed hearts.

People who were addicts.
Liars.
Broken.
Ashamed.

Now forgiven.
Now free.
Now alive in Him.
And the center is not rules.
It’s Jesus.

Crucified.
Risen.
Calling your name.

So if what you’ve seen feels like cold religion—
don’t walk away from Christ because of what man built around Him.
Run to Him.

He’s still building His church.
One transformed life at a time.
Including yours.

If this stirred something in you, don’t ignore it.
This might be your moment to stop performing… and start surrendering.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You do not call it evil.
paragraphs:
You do not call it evil.
You call it understandable.
That is how the heart hides.
Isaiah 5:20 does not whisper. It warns: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.”

Not those who accidentally stumbled.
Those who renamed sin so they could sleep beside it.

We do it more than we admit.
Bitterness becomes “boundaries.”
Lust becomes “need.”
Pride becomes “confidence.”
Disobedience becomes “peace.”
And what God clearly confronted, we decorate with softer words so conscience stops shouting.
But here’s what we miss…

The danger is not only in doing wrong.
The deeper danger is justifying what we already know is wrong.
Because once you baptize rebellion with nice language, repentance starts to feel unnecessary.
That is a deadly place.

Sin does not become safe because culture applauds it.
Darkness does not become light because your feelings defend it.
And a lie does not become truth because you repeated it long enough.
But grace walks in right there.

Jesus did not come for people who had no sin.
He came for people honest enough to stop hiding it.
The cross is not for the self-excused.
It is for the broken, the convicted, the surrendering.
When you call sin what God calls it, you are not losing freedom — you are finally stepping into it.

So stop renaming what God has already revealed.
Drop the excuse.
Break agreement with the lie.
Come clean before the Lord.

There is mercy for the one who repents.
There is cleansing for the one who confesses.
There is no shame too deep that the blood of Jesus cannot wash.

Call it what it is.
Then bring it to Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was doing everything right…
paragraphs:
She was doing everything right…
and still missed what mattered most.

Martha was moving.
Mary was still.
In Luke 10:38–42, the house is full, the pressure is real, and expectations are loud. Martha is serving, hustling, carrying the weight of responsibility. Plates. Preparations. Perfection.
And then—she snaps.
“Lord, don’t You care?”

That line doesn’t come from laziness.
It comes from overload.

From doing so much for Jesus…
that she stopped being with Him.
But here’s what we miss—

Martha wasn’t rebuked for serving.
She was corrected for being consumed.
“You are anxious and troubled about many things…”

Not evil things.
Not sinful things.
Just… too many things.
Meanwhile, Mary chose something radical.
She sat.

At His feet.
Eyes locked.
Heart open.
Noise silenced.
And Jesus says something that cuts through centuries:
“Mary has chosen the better part…”

Not the easier part.
The better part.

Stillness isn’t weakness.
It’s warfare.

Because the enemy doesn’t just tempt you with sin—
he distracts you with busyness.

So you look productive…
but feel empty.

You look faithful…
but feel far.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Jesus doesn’t shame Martha.
He invites her.

Away from anxiety.
Back to intimacy.

Because the Gospel isn’t: “Do more for God.”
It’s: “Come be with Me.”

Before the cross, before the resurrection, even here—
Jesus was already restoring distracted hearts.
And at the cross, He finished it.

Your worth is not in your workload.
Your acceptance is not in your activity.
Your peace is not in your performance.
It’s in Christ alone.
So pause.
Sit.
Listen.

He’s not asking for more effort.
He’s asking for your attention.

From anxiety to intimacy—
because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He wasn’t told to admire faith.
paragraphs: He wasn’t told to admire faith.
He was told to fight for it.
“Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called…” — 1 Timothy 6:12

That means faith is not passive.
It bleeds.
It wrestles.
It stands when everything in you wants to quit.

Because some battles are not with swords.
They are with temptation.
Fear.
Secret compromise.
The voices that whisper, “Just give up. Just blend in. Just bow once.”
But here’s what we miss:

Paul did not say fight for popularity.
Fight for comfort.
Fight for applause.
He said fight the good fight of faith.

The good fight is the battle to keep trusting Jesus when money seduces, when lust stalks, when suffering confuses, and when your own heart feels tired. It is the war of holding on to Christ when the world offers cheaper saviors.
And you do not fight alone.

Jesus already won the decisive victory at the cross. He crushed sin’s claim, broke death’s sting, and rose again so weary sinners could stand in grace, not in their own strength. We fight from His victory, not for it.

So today, brother. Sister.
Do not surrender your soul for a temporary escape.

Pray again.
Repent again.
Stand again.
Believe again.

This is not the hour to drift.
This is the hour to take hold of eternal life and refuse to let hell, shame, or desire drag you back.

Fight.
Not with pride.
Not with panic.
But with faith in the Son of God.

And when your hands shake, remember:
the same Christ who calls you to fight is the Christ who keeps you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From The Ministry of Johanna
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From The Ministry of Johanna

She wasn’t loud.
She didn’t trend.
But heaven paid attention.
Johanna.
But I didn’t.
Because her ministry whispered something my soul needed—and it exposed something I didn’t want to face.

She didn’t preach on platforms.
She didn’t build crowds.
She didn’t fight for visibility.
She served.

Quietly.
Faithfully.
Costly.
Luke 8:3 tells us she used her own resources to support Jesus’ ministry.

Not leftovers.
Not convenience.
Her substance.
Her life.
And that’s where it hit me.

I wanted impact…
without sacrifice.

I wanted influence…
without surrender.

I wanted God to use me—
but on my terms.
But here’s what we miss…

The Kingdom of God isn’t sustained by spotlight.
It’s sustained by surrendered hearts.
Johanna teaches us this:

You don’t have to be seen to be significant.
You don’t have to be famous to be faithful.
You don’t have to hold the mic to move heaven.
And here’s the Gospel.

We were all once like that—
giving God fragments…
half-hearted devotion…
selective obedience.
But Christ didn’t give us a portion.
He gave everything.

On the cross, Jesus poured out His life—
not quietly ignored, but brutally displayed—
so that our hidden, broken offerings could be redeemed.
And now?
We don’t serve to be seen.
We serve because we’ve been saved.
We give because He first gave.
We surrender because grace found us in our smallness and called it enough.
So here’s the lesson Johanna burned into my heart:

Faithfulness in secret
is never invisible to God.

And the same Jesus she supported…
is the same Savior calling you today.
Not to be famous.
But to be His.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t raise his voice.
paragraphs:
He didn’t raise his voice.
He lowered his heart.
And that’s what made heaven listen.
5 Attitudes That Reveal a Humble Heart

You choose repentance over reputation.
You stop defending your image… and start confessing your sin.
Not polished prayers.
Broken ones.
Like David in Psalm 51—no excuses, just surrender.
You listen more than you speak.
Pride interrupts.
Humility leans in.
Even when correction stings, you don’t shut down—you bow low enough to grow.
You serve when no one is watching.
No applause.
No spotlight.
Just obedience.
Because your reward isn’t the crowd… it’s Christ.
You give God credit for everything good.
Not “I did this.”
But “God carried me through.”
You remember: every gift, every win, every breath—grace, not entitlement.
You depend on God daily, not just in crisis.
Humble hearts don’t wait for collapse before they kneel.
They live surrendered.
Every day.
Every decision.
“Lord, I need You”—not as a last resort, but as a lifestyle.
But here’s what we miss…

Humility isn’t thinking less of yourself.
It’s seeing yourself rightly before a holy God.
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because Scripture says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Not because the humble are perfect—
but because they know they’re not.
That’s the Gospel.

We were proud.
We were lost.
We tried to be our own saviors.
And Jesus stepped in.

He humbled Himself to the cross—
took our sin, our shame, our rebellion—
and offered us something we could never earn:
Grace.
Forgiveness.
New life.

So today—drop the mask.
Lower the heart.
Run to Christ.

Because the ground at the foot of the cross?
It’s level.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… secret gatherings strengthened courage publicly?
paragraphs: Did you know… secret gatherings strengthened courage publicly?
They whispered… while the world watched in silence.
Doors locked. Lamps low. Hearts pounding.
And yet—that’s where courage was born.

In the shadows, believers gathered. Not for comfort. Not for show.
But for survival… and surrender.

Look at Acts of the Apostles.
The early church didn’t start on stages—it started in rooms. Hidden spaces. Upper chambers.

They prayed.
They broke bread.
They trembled.

Because outside those doors?
Threats. Prison. Death.
But here’s what we miss…

Those secret gatherings didn’t weaken them—
they forged them.

In private, they met Jesus again and again.
In quiet, they were filled with the Spirit.
In hiding, they found a boldness the world couldn’t explain.
So when they stepped out?
They didn’t whisper anymore.

They preached in streets.
They stood before rulers.
They chose obedience over safety.
Read Acts of the Apostles 4:31—after they prayed, “the place was shaken… and they spoke the word of God boldly.”
Boldly.
The same men who once hid… now stood unshaken.
Why?

Because courage isn’t manufactured in public.
It’s birthed in the presence of God.
And that points us to the Gospel.

Jesus Himself—
betrayed in the dark,
crucified in public,
rose in power.
Our Savior didn’t avoid the shadows—He redeemed them.

Your secret place matters.
Your unseen prayers matter.
Your quiet surrender?
Heaven sees it all.
And one day, that hidden faith will stand in the light—unashamed, unshaken, alive in Christ.

If this stirred something in you… don’t ignore it.
Step back into the secret place.
Because public courage begins where no one else is watching.
From hidden rooms to holy fire—because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: People missed that Abraham laughed at God’s promise too (Genesis 17:17)
paragraphs: People missed that Abraham laughed at God’s promise too (Genesis 17:17)
Exactly.
Sarah wasn’t the only one who laughed.

Abraham laughed too.
Face down. Old body. Impossible promise.
And in that moment, even the father of faith blinked at the size of God’s word.
Genesis 17:17 does not hide it. Abraham laughed and said in his heart, “Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” The Bible is honest about its heroes. That matters.

Because faith is not pretending you never stagger.
Faith is hearing the impossible… and still staying under the voice of God until the promise becomes bigger than your doubt.
But here’s what people miss.

Abraham laughed.
Sarah laughed.
Yet God still moved.

Not because their faith was flawless.
Because His covenant was.

That is the Gospel pattern all over Scripture. We tremble. We question. We fail. But God remains faithful. He does not save perfect people. He keeps His word to weak people through His own power. And that story reaches its fullness in Jesus Christ—the promised Son through whom barren hearts become alive again.

So yes, Abraham laughed.
And grace did not walk away.

It stayed.
It spoke again.
It fulfilled what human strength could never produce.

That means your moment of weakness does not have to be the end of your story. Bring your unbelief to God. Bring your fear to Christ. Repent of cynicism, yes—but do not run from Him. The same God who answered Abraham has given us an even greater promise in Jesus: forgiveness for sinners, new life for the dead soul, and hope that does not collapse under impossibility.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: It feels right.
paragraphs:
It feels right.
It must be right.
That’s the lie.

“Follow your heart,” they said.
But Jeremiah 17:9 cuts through the noise like a blade:
“The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick—who can understand it?”

Not weak.
Not confused.
Deceitful.

We don’t like that verse.
Because it confronts the one thing we trust the most—ourselves.

Your heart can feel love… and lead you into lust.
It can crave freedom… and drag you into bondage.
It can whisper “this will make you happy”… while quietly destroying your soul.
And here’s the tension:

Your feelings are real.
But they are not reliable.
But here’s what we miss…

God never told you to follow your heart.
He told you to guard it.

Proverbs 4:23:
“Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.”

Guard it—from lies.
From unchecked desires.
From voices that sound like truth but aren’t.

Because if your heart is the compass…
and it’s broken…
you won’t end up where you think.
And that’s where grace walks in.

God doesn’t leave you trapped in a deceitful heart.
He offers you a new one.

Ezekiel 36:26:
“I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you.”

Not repaired.
Replaced.

Through Jesus Christ—His death, His resurrection—your old, wandering heart can be made new.
Not driven by impulse, but led by truth.
Not enslaved to desire, but anchored in Him.
So no—don’t follow your heart.

Lead it.
Submit it.
Surrender it to Christ.

Because the safest place your heart can be…
is not in your feelings—
but in His hands.
From deception to redemption—because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Busy in ministry. Empty in spirit.
paragraphs:
Busy in ministry. Empty in spirit.
That is one of the most dangerous places a believer can stand—holding the microphone while quietly losing the oil.

You can preach and still be prayerless.
Serve and still be starving.
Lead worship and still feel no wonder.
Open your Bible for sermons… but not for your own soul.

That is not just exhaustion.
That is a warning.
Martha was busy with much serving, but Mary sat at the feet of Jesus. And Jesus did not shame service—He exposed distraction. “One thing is necessary” (Luke 10:38–42).

Some ministers are drowning in church work while neglecting Christ Himself.
Public fire.
Private ashes.
But here’s what we miss…

Jesus does not call the weary servant away to condemn him.
He calls him back to Himself.
“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

You do not need a better schedule before you need a Savior.
You need repentance.
You need presence.
You need to stop confusing activity with intimacy.

Ministry without communion becomes performance.
Service without devotion becomes noise.
But when you return to Jesus, the burden lifts, the soul breathes, and the secret place becomes sweet again.

Brother, sister—God never asked you to carry His work without His presence.
Sit again at His feet.
Weep if you must.
Be still long enough for your heart to remember who you were serving in the first place.

You are not saved by ministry.
You are saved by Christ.
And the same Jesus who called you to serve is still calling you to abide.
Don’t just work for Him. Walk with Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They didn’t just lose a battle.
paragraphs: They didn’t just lose a battle.
They were erased.
Men. Women. Children. Entire nations wiped out—and it was God who commanded it.
That tension should shake you.
Because this is the same God who says, “Love your enemies.”
So what’s going on?
Here’s what we miss…

God wasn’t acting out of rage.
He was executing judgment after centuries of mercy.

In Genesis 15:16, God tells Abraham something chilling:
The sin of the Canaanites “has not yet reached its full measure.”
Translation?
Judgment was delayed.
For hundreds of years.

These nations weren’t innocent villages.
They practiced brutal evil—child sacrifice, ritual violence, corruption that poisoned everything.
By the time you reach Deuteronomy and Joshua, this wasn’t sudden.
It was final.
But here’s where grace walks in.
Even in judgment… God made a way out.
A prostitute named Rahab—living in that doomed city—chose to believe.
And God spared her.
Not just spared.
He redeemed her story and placed her in the lineage of Jesus (see Matthew 1).
Let that sink in.
In the middle of destruction, mercy was still available.
So what does this mean for us?
God is not cruel.
He is holy.
And holiness confronts evil—fully, finally, justly.
But He is also patient.
And right now, you’re living in that patience.
Because the same God who judged nations…
Sent His Son to be judged for you.
At the cross, wrath and mercy collided.
Jesus took the destruction we deserved.
This isn’t just history.
It’s a warning.
And an invitation.

Judgment is real.
But so is grace.
Turn while there’s still time.
Run to Christ—not away from Him.

Because from scandal to grace—
Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They won’t hear the Gospel… because you chose comfort.
paragraphs: They won’t hear the Gospel… because you chose comfort.
Silence feels harmless.
But it isn’t.
It’s eternal.
Somewhere right now, someone you know is one breath away from eternity—and they’ve never heard that Jesus Christ died for them.

Not clearly.
Not personally.
Not urgently.
And heaven is not automatic.

Hell is real.
Sin is deadly.
And neutrality… is a decision.
“How will they believe in Him of whom they have not heard?” — Romans 10:14
Let that sit.

You’re not just quiet.
You’re withholding the cure while the disease spreads.
But here’s what we miss…
Evangelism is not about being perfect.
It’s about being rescued.

You don’t need a microphone.
You need a testimony.

You don’t need a stage.
You need surrender.
Because the Gospel is simple:

We sinned.
We rebelled.
We deserved judgment.
But Jesus Christ stepped in—took the wrath, carried the cross, and rose again—so anyone who repents and believes in Him will not perish but have eternal life.

That includes your friend.
Your sibling.
Your coworker.
Yes—that one you keep avoiding.
And that’s where grace walks in.
God is not asking you to save them.
He’s asking you to speak.

To love them enough to risk awkwardness.
To open your mouth even when your voice shakes.
Because eternity is louder than your fear.
So wake up, believer.

Not with guilt—
but with fire.

Not with pressure—
but with purpose.
Someone’s forever may be hanging on your obedience today.
Message someone. Pray for someone. Speak to someone.
And trust that the same Jesus who saved you… is still saving.
From silence to salvation.
Because grace was never meant to be hidden.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… the early Church didn’t start with power?
paragraphs: Did you know… the early Church didn’t start with power?
It started with unity.

Not miracles first.
Not influence.
Not numbers.
Unity.
“They were all together in one place…” (Acts 2:1)
That’s where heaven touched earth.

Before the fire fell…
Before 3,000 were saved…
Before the bold preaching…
There was a room full of people who chose each other over ego.

No platforms.
No titles.
No competition.
Just hearts aligned under one Name—Jesus.
But here’s what we miss…
We chase power without protecting unity.

We want the anointing…
But we resist forgiveness.
We want revival…
But we harbor offense.
We want God to move…
But we won’t reconcile.
And heaven waits.
Because the Spirit doesn’t rest on division.
Psalm 133 says unity is where God commands the blessing.

Not suggests.
Commands.
And that blessing? It’s life. It’s presence. It’s power.

So when the disciples humbled themselves…
Prayed together…
Stayed together…
That’s when the fire came.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because unity is not something we manufacture.
It’s something Jesus died to create.

On the cross, He didn’t just forgive you—
He tore down the walls between us.

Sin divides.
Christ restores.

And the same Spirit that fell in Acts 2?
He still moves today—
But He’s looking for hearts that are surrendered, not superior.
So let me ask you…

Who do you need to forgive?
What pride do you need to lay down?
Where has division replaced devotion?
Come back.

Not just to power—
But to the posture that invites it.

Unity.
Humility.
Jesus at the center.
Because revival doesn’t begin on a stage.
It begins in a surrendered heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The righteous will live by faith — Habakkuk 2
paragraphs: The righteous will live by faith — Habakkuk 2
Heaven shook a nation with one line:

“The righteous will live by faith.”
— Habakkuk 2:4

Babylon looked powerful.
Proud.
Untouchable.
And Judah looked weak, frightened, collapsing under judgment.

But God was not impressed by noise.
He was watching the heart.

The proud soul swells up.
It trusts its own strength.
Its own timing.
Its own control.
But the righteous?
They live by faith.

Not by visibility.
Not by feelings.
Not by applause.
Not by what the bank account says.
Not by what the doctor said.
Not by how dark the night feels.
By faith.

And here’s what we miss: Habakkuk 2:4 is not a motivational slogan. It is a dividing line. One path is pride. The other is trust. One says, “I can carry myself.” The other says, “Lord, if You don’t hold me, I fall.”
This is why the Gospel matters.

Because none of us are righteous on our own.
We are not saved by strong faith in ourselves.
We are saved by faith in Jesus Christ — the truly Righteous One who died for sinners, rose again, and gives His righteousness to those who repent and believe.

So yes, the righteous live by faith.
But only because Christ first died for the unrighteous.
That is grace.
That is mercy.
That is our hope.

So breathe, kapatid.
If life feels uncertain, God’s Word is not.
If your hands are shaking, Christ is still steady.
Walk by faith.
Cling to Jesus.
The same God who spoke through Habakkuk still keeps His people now.
Don’t let fear disciple you. Let faith do it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… some believers memorized Scripture because copies were rare?
paragraphs: Did you know… some believers memorized Scripture because copies were rare?
They didn’t scroll.
They stored the Word… in their bones.
Because they had no Bible in their hands.
Only fire in their hearts.
Some believers in the early Church couldn’t just open an app or grab a printed copy. Scripture was rare. Expensive. Sometimes dangerous to carry. So they did something we’ve forgotten how to do—
They memorized it.

Line by line.
Word by word.
Tears included.

David said it first:
“I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You.” (Psalm 119:11)
Hidden.

Not highlighted.
Not bookmarked.
Hidden.
But here’s what we miss…
They didn’t memorize Scripture to impress people.
They memorized it to survive.

Because when persecution came…
When fear whispered…
When temptation screamed…
They had a voice louder than all of it:
God’s Word—alive inside them.
And that’s where grace walks in.
You can own five Bibles and still be empty.
Or carry one verse in your heart… and be unshakable.
Jesus Himself fought temptation not with power displays—but with written Word remembered (Matthew 4:4).
So the question hits deep:
What’s stored in you when life squeezes you?
Because whatever fills your heart… will spill in your storm.
Today, don’t just read Scripture.
Carry it.

Repeat it.
Pray it.
Live it.
Let it move from your screen… into your soul.
And when you fail—and we all do—remember this:
The same Word that convicts you… is the same Word that leads you back to Jesus.
Grace is not far.
It’s already speaking.
Sit with one verse today.
From distraction to devotion—because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Jesus Wrote on the Ground — John 8:6
paragraphs: Why Jesus Wrote on the Ground — John 8:6

They dragged her into the light.
Caught. Exposed. No defense left.

And in the middle of the noise—
He bent down.
Silence.

In Gospel of John 8:6, when the trap was set and the stones were ready, Jesus Christ didn’t argue first.
He didn’t shout.
He wrote on the ground.
Why?

Scripture doesn’t record the words.
And that’s where the tension breathes.

Some scholars interpret that He wrote the accusers’ sins—names, secrets, hidden things they thought no one saw.
Others see an echo of Jeremiah 17:13—those who turn away from God will be written in the dust.
Dust. Temporary. Fading.
But here’s what we miss—

While they were holding stones,
He was lowering Himself to the ground.

Not to condemn.
But to confront without crushing.

Not to expose her shame—
But theirs.
One by one, the stones dropped.

Oldest first.
Because the longer you live, the more you know your own dirt.
And when the crowd disappeared, He stood back up.

“Woman, where are they?”
“No one, Lord.”
“Then neither do I condemn you… go, and sin no more.” (John 8:10–11)
That’s the Gospel.

Not denial of sin.
Not approval of sin.
But grace that disarms the executioners and transforms the accused.

He wrote in the dirt—
because He was about to rewrite a life.
And maybe… yours too.

You feel exposed?
Ashamed?
Like your story is already decided?
Look again.

The same hand that wrote in the dust
was nailed to a cross for you.

Your sin may be written in the dirt—
but your redemption is written in His blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did you know… Jesus spoke in parables that not everyone understood?
paragraphs: Did you know… Jesus spoke in parables that not everyone understood?

They heard the same words…
but walked away with completely different hearts.
Jesus didn’t hide truth.

He revealed it—
but only to those who were ready to surrender.
In Matthew 13, when Jesus Christ told the Parable of the Sower, the crowd leaned in.

Stories about seeds.
Soil.
Farming.
Simple, right?
But then He said something that shook everything:
“Whoever has ears, let them hear.”

Wait—
they all had ears.
So what did He mean?
The disciples asked Him privately, and Jesus answered with weight:

Some hear… but never understand.
Some see… but never perceive.
Why?

Because truth isn’t just heard.
It’s received.
And here’s the tension—don’t miss this:

Parables didn’t just reveal truth.
They exposed hearts.

Hard hearts hear stories and stay unchanged.
Hungry hearts hear God and fall to their knees.

Same message.
Different soil.
But here’s what we miss…
Jesus wasn’t trying to confuse people.
He was separating curiosity from surrender.

Because the Kingdom of God isn’t unlocked by intelligence—
it’s opened by repentance.
That’s the Gospel.

We were the hardened ground.
Closed. Resistant. Wandering.
But Jesus didn’t leave us there.

Through the cross, He broke the soil.
Through His blood, He planted grace.
Through His resurrection, He offers new life.

Now the question isn’t:
“Do you understand the story?”
It’s this:
Will you let the Word change you?
Today, don’t just listen.
Receive.

Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
And watch your life bear fruit you could never grow on your own.

From hidden truth to revealed grace—
because Jesus still speaks to those who are listening.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Acts 17:28
paragraphs: Acts 17:28
“For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.” — KJV
Brother, this verse hits like thunder wrapped in mercy.

Paul is telling Athens: You are not self-made.
Not self-sustained.
Not self-owned.

In Him you breathe.
In Him you stand.
In Him your next heartbeat is possible.

That means pride has to bow.
But despair has to bow too.

Because if your life is held in God’s hands, then your story is not random. You are not floating through chaos unseen. Even in rebellion, even in confusion, even in a city full of idols, Paul points people back to the God who is near, not far.
But here is what we must not miss:

Acts 17:28 is not saying everyone is automatically saved.
It is saying every human being depends on God completely.
And that reality should lead us to repentance and faith in Christ.
A few verses later, Paul calls all people everywhere to repent because God has appointed a day of judgment through the risen Jesus. So the verse is beautiful, yes—but it is also a wake-up call.

You live because of Him.
Now the question is:
Are you living for Him?

Jesus is not just the source of life.
He is the Savior who rescues ruined lives.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose again.
The One who gives meaning, forgiveness, and a future.

Acts 17:28 in one line:
You are alive by God’s power, and you are called to return to God through Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t fall when Delilah cut his hair.
paragraphs: He didn’t fall when Delilah cut his hair.
He was already falling… long before the scissors touched his head.

Judges 16 doesn’t start with betrayal.
It starts with compromise.

Samson kept stepping into places God warned him about.
Closer.
Darker.
Riskier.

Until sin stopped feeling dangerous…
and started feeling normal.

Delilah didn’t destroy Samson.
She just exposed what Samson refused to confront.
And here’s what we miss—

His strength didn’t leave in a moment.
It eroded in silence.

Every secret.
Every flirtation with disobedience.
Every “I can handle this.”

Chip.
By chip.
By chip.

Until the anointing he carried…
was no longer the life he lived.

Judges 16:20 hits like thunder:
“He did not know that the Lord had left him.”

Not because God is cruel—
but because Samson kept choosing distance.

Sin doesn’t usually ambush you.
It recruits you.
Slowly.
Patiently.
Personally.
But here’s where grace walks in.

Samson’s story didn’t end in failure.
Blinded. Broken. Chained—yes.
But not abandoned.

In his lowest place, he finally prayed.
Not for pleasure. Not for pride.
But for God.
And God answered.

One last time.
